No apps named 'Shvilist', 'Israel Trail Guide by Jacob Saar' or 'INT by Eli' were found. No dedicated app for trail angels or water caching was found.
התמונה בשוק (נובמבר 2026): יש בדיוק אפלי: The market picture (November 2026): there is exactly one dedicated Israel National Trail app – 'Israel National Trail' by Lior Boyango – free, offline, with sections, water, campsites and self-managed trail angels, and a high rating (4.5–4.7). It is a good field companion but has almost no planning layer: no daily itinerary, no water/heat/daylight calculations, no journal, no export. Against it stand general map apps: Israel Hiking Map/Mapeak (the best map in Israel, open source, route planning and recording, but offline costs ILS 99.90 per year and zero trail logistics), and Amud Anan (a huge community POI database but a 3.1 rating, crashes, abandoned iOS, paid maps). The global apps (Wikiloc, AllTrails, Komoot, HiiKER, FarOut) cover the trail partially or as user routes, lock offline/alerts/live sharing behind subscriptions of ILS 80–300 per year, and have no Hebrew, angels, caches or official overnight campsites – although FarOut offers an excellent model of dated comments on every water point, AllTrails/Off-Road offer live location sharing, and HiiKER a division into stages with amenities. SPNI has not released an official app; the official information (52 maps, angel list, route changes) is scattered across PDFs and web pages. The recurring complaints everywhere: paid offline, battery drain, outdated angel phone numbers, water info going stale, no planner, no watch support, and apps that depend on a single developer. The big gap: no tool connects planning (daily, water, caches, angels, Shabbat, daylight, heat/floods) with field guidance and logging – and that is exactly what our PWA is already starting to do.

\"מלאכי שביל\" הם תושבים ביישובים לאורך: "Trail angels" are residents of communities along the Israel National Trail route who have chosen to host hikers, usually for free or for a token payment. The phenomenon grew with the trail's rising popularity, and SPNI (the Israel Trails Committee) maintains an official list divided by region, from Dan to Eilat. According to ISRAEL21c the network currently numbers about 450–500 hosts (in 2012 there were about 100 registered). What they offer: in most cases a shower, a spot for a tent in the yard or a mattress/bed in a room, water, phone charging; some offer laundry, a hot meal, coffee, and sometimes a yurt/cabin dedicated to hikers (for example the 'Angels' Cabin' in Sansana, the hikers' cabin in Tzukim). Some hosts offer only a shower/water without lodging (according to SPNI guidelines, hosting without lodging or a shower is not included in the official list). Cost: most angels ask for nothing; some ask for a token donation (according to Bex Band: 20–80 ILS per person when they ask); according to shvil.fandom, places charging up to ~15 ILS are still listed in the angels list, and above that they are considered 'cheap paid lodging'. In the Negev some of the 'services' (meals in Shaharut, shuttles, water caching) are paid. Making contact: phone/WhatsApp in advance (preferably by message, 24–48 hours ahead, not late at night); in some communities (for example Kibbutz Dan) you temporarily join the community's WhatsApp group and write your arrival date, number of people and what you need. The lists change frequently — hosts stop hosting, so always verify. The SPNI list is updated by the hosts themselves by email at shvil@spni.org.il or via WhatsApp. For English-speaking hikers: israeltrail.net maintains a list in English (it claims to be the only up-to-date one), and shvil.fandom.com (INT Trail Angels) and israelbylocals.com also present lists — but they themselves note that they are not managed by the angels and are not necessarily up to date.

The convention: when the white stripe 'leads'/is on top – you are heading north (toward the snowy Hermon); when the orange leads – south (toward the Negev). The later you leave (after mid-March), the more you risk sharav and heat of 35°C+ in the Arava and the makhteshim even before reaching Arad. Another advantage: the days get longer over the course of the trek.

Do not cache in a streambed (flash floods), and do not mark too conspicuously (theft/animals).

Never enter a flowing streambed, never camp overnight in a streambed, and on flash-flood warning days (Meteorological Service / INPA) avoid the wadis of the Judean Desert, the Negev and the Arava.
באביב צפונה (NOBO): בורחים מהחום שמתקרב: Northbound in spring (NOBO): you escape the heat approaching the Negev and reach a green Galilee with long days. Southbound in autumn (SOBO): the north is still dry and you reach the Negev after the heat breaks, but with short days and flash-flood risk. Most Israeli hikers choose northbound in spring.

צפע ארץ-ישראלי בצפון ובמרכז (מרץ–נובמבר): Palestine viper in the north and centre (March–November) – don't turn over stones, wear high boots, use a headlamp at night; if bitten – call 101, no tourniquet. Scorpions in the Negev – shake out shoes and gear in the morning. Hyenas and jackals are usually not dangerous – keep food sealed. Ticks in spring – check daily.
בצפון ובמרכז: ברזיות ביישובים, בתי עלמין: In the north and centre: drinking fountains in localities, cemeteries, petrol stations, field schools (Hermon, Meron? – check), springs (Ein Tina, Ein Koren, Nahal Amud, Ein Hemed) – spring water must be purified/filtered (leptospirosis and bacteria). KKL-JNF overnight campsites (e.g. in the Carmel and the Shephelah) usually have no tap.
אוטובוסים מאילת: אגד 390 לתל אביב (~5 שע: Buses from Eilat: Egged 390 to Tel Aviv (~5 hours), 444 to Jerusalem (~4.5–5 hours), 397 to Beer Sheva (via Ramon Airport and Dimona), 392/394 to Beer Sheva/Tel Aviv via the Arava or Mitzpe Ramon. Booking a seat in advance is recommended (egged.co.il or the Egged app) – especially on Saturday nights and holidays.
רשות הטבע והגנים: 4–6 ליטר לאדם ליום לשת: Israel Nature and Parks Authority: 4–6 litres per person per day for drinking alone. SPNI: 3–4 litres per day in the north and centre, 5–6 litres in the south; hikers report 6–7 litres on a hot day in the Arava (including cooking). Recommended carrying capacity: 4–6 litres (up to 8–9 litres when setting out on two-day stretches without water).
שלג יורד כמעט מדי חורף בחרמון (מקטעי הפת: Snow falls almost every winter on the Hermon (the opening sections from the Hermon to Tel Hai; the Hermon site closes to hikers in snow) and sometimes on Mount Meron (1,200 m) and in Safed – usually December–February, for a few days. A SOBO hiker leaving in October avoids it; a NOBO hiker reaching Meron in April will almost never meet snow.
צפע ארץ-ישראלי (Daboia palaestinae) – ~9: Palestine viper (Daboia palaestinae) – ~90% of venomous bites in Israel; especially active March–November and on summer nights. In the north and centre. Don't turn over stones, don't reach into crevices, wear high boots, use a headlamp at night. If bitten: stay calm, immobilize, call 101 – no tourniquet, no sucking, no ice.
שבת: מכניסת שבת (ו' לפנות ערב) עד צאת הש: Shabbat: from the start of Shabbat (Friday towards evening) until it ends (Saturday night) – no public transport, supermarkets and grocery stores in Jewish localities are closed (kibbutz grocery stores are usually closed on Friday afternoon too). Druze villages (Isfiya, Daliyat al-Karmel, Majdal Shams) and Arab villages – open; petrol stations on main roads are open.
אין מסורת של 'חבילות דואר' כמו בארה\"ב –: There is no tradition of 'mail drops' as in the US – distances are short and there are supermarkets. You can send a parcel via Israel Post/couriers to a post office or to a trail angel in Arad/Mitzpe Ramon (by arrangement), or leave gear with a trail angel. A 'desert kit' (jerrycans, food for 10 days) is usually brought to Arad/Mitzpe Ramon by car before the trek.
קטעי החרמון–תל חי (38 ק\"מ, נפתחו 2023): The Hermon–Tel Hai sections (38 km, opened 2023) were closed during the war (2023–2025) and reopened gradually; the Hermon site reopened in March 2025. In October 2026 the route north of Kiryat Shmona was temporarily diverted (Tel Hai–Kfar Giladi bridge works). Before heading out: check SPNI and INPA updates and the Home Front Command app.
ההליכה בשביל 'נחלקת לערד ואחרי ערד': מצפ: Hiking the trail 'divides into Arad and after Arad': north of Arad there is a locality, a drinking fountain or a spring almost every day; south of Arad (sections ~33–56 in SPNI's numbering, about 350 km) water sources are sparse and caches or a caching service are needed. The typical number of caches between Arad and Eilat: 6–8 (shvil wiki: 'on average 7 caches').
אוקטובר 2023 – 2025: קטעי הצפון (חרמון,: October 2023 – 2025: the northern sections (Hermon, Tel Hai, Upper Galilee near the Lebanese border) and the Gaza border area (not on the route) were closed/restricted under Home Front Command guidelines; bus lines in the Upper Galilee (e.g. line 36 Kiryat Shmona–Dan–Snir) were cancelled 'until further notice'. Most 2024 hikers started/finished at Tel Hai or further south.
מדרום לערד ועד אילת (כ-350 ק\"מ): בין ער: From south of Arad to Eilat (about 350 km): between Arad and the Zin Works, around the Hava/Mador campsites (Sde Boker–Mitzpe Ramon), Gev Holit, and elsewhere – on average 6–8 caches. INPA campsites with a tap (Nekarot West, Barak, Tzihor, Beer Milhan, Raham-Etek, Shehoret, Yehoram, Gevanim, Hod Akev, Mitzpe Makhtesh) make things easier but are no substitute for a backup.
שטחי אש (שטחי אימונים של צה\"ל) מכסים כ-: Firing zones (IDF training areas) cover about 7,500 sq km of the Negev. SPNI's rule: 'Hiking in firing zones requires coordination, and is usually possible only on weekends'. Coordination is required on Shabbat and holidays too – 'weekends only' is not an exemption from coordination. Check on a trail map (Israel Hiking Map shows firing zones with red hatching) whether the section crosses a firing zone.
מלאכי שביל (Trail Angels): תושבים לאורך: Trail angels: residents along the trail who host hikers for the night, a shower, laundry and food free of charge (or for a token fee) and help with water caching and shuttles. It is customary to call a day or two in advance, arrive as clean as possible, and leave the place clean. The updated list in English – israeltrail.net; in Hebrew – the shvil wiki and the Facebook groups.
The Israel National Trail is a winter-spring and autumn trail. The two accepted windows: northbound (NOBO) – leaving Eilat from late January to mid-March and finishing on the Hermon in April–May; southbound (SOBO) – leaving the Hermon/Dan in October to early November and finishing in Eilat in December–January. Do not attempt a full thru-hike in summer (June–September): the Negev and the Arava are life-threatening in the heat.
להוריד מראש: שכבת מפה לא-מקוונת (Israel: Download in advance: an offline map layer (Israel Hiking Map with a subscription, or Amud Anan, or OsmAnd/Organic Maps with the Israel map + the trail GPX), the official GPX for each section from SPNI, and the coordinates file of the water caches. Battery: a 10,000–20,000mAh power bank, airplane mode during the day; no reception in parts of the craters and in the Arava. A paper map of the Negev as backup.
חגים: ראש השנה ויום כיפור (ספטמבר/אוקטוב: Holidays: Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur (September/October – on Yom Kippur there is no traffic at all), Sukkot (a week of holidays – overnight campsites crowded and firing zones sometimes open), Passover (April – a week; leavened products not sold in many supermarkets), Independence Day (May – crowds outdoors, barbecues), Shavuot, Lag BaOmer (Meron – hundreds of thousands, the section near the tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is crowded/closed).
בודקים ב-Israel Hiking Map (שטחי אש בקוו: Check on Israel Hiking Map (firing zones in red hatching) and on the section page on the SPNI website. The rule: hiking in a firing zone requires coordination with the Command's coordination office (South: 08-9902926/8, about two weeks in advance), and is usually possible only on weekends and holidays. Main sections: Nahal Tzihor–Shizafon, Paran/Tzihor–Shittim, Neot Smadar–Shaharut. Do not stray from the markings; unexploded ordnance – don't touch, call 100.
לפי רשות הטבע והגנים (parks.org.il/new/s: According to the Israel Nature and Parks Authority (parks.org.il/new/shvil-israel), overnight campsites with a drinking water supply in the southern part: Yehoram, Shehoret, Raham-Etek, Beer Milhan, Nahal Tzihor, Nahal Barak, Nekarot West, Nahal Gevanim, Hod Akev, Mitzpe Makhtesh (near Mitzpe Ramon). Open free of charge and without coordination; the water is for drinking only (not for showering/laundry). The taps are sometimes shut off – do not rely on a single tap without a backup.
מקטעי הפתיחה (כניסת אתר החרמון – נווה אט: The opening sections (Hermon site entrance – Neve Ativ – Nimrod – Tel Hai, ~38 km, opened August 2023) pass close to fenced minefields (yellow fence/red sign – do not cross), through military areas and near the border. Snow and ice in winter; the Hermon site closes to visitors during storms. During the war (October 2023 – 2025) the area was closed to hikers; the Hermon site reopened in March 2025. Check Home Front Command/INPA notices before heading out.
כלל הכיוון (Wikivoyage ומדריכים): כשהפס: The direction rule (Wikivoyage and guidebooks): when the white stripe is on top/leading – you are heading north; when the orange stripe is on top/leading – you are heading south. That is: in a 'regular' horizontal blaze the white is on top and the orange at the bottom; when the blaze is tilted/painted so that the orange is at the front end, the direction is south (to Eilat). This is a field convention, not a binding rule – in practice the decision is made by map/GPS, and the blaze only confirms you are on the trail. Arrows/double blazes mark a turn.

עין עֹבדת הוא מעיין בהר הנגב, הנובע בנחל: Ein Avdat is a spring in the Negev Highlands, rising in Nahal Zin and designated a national park.
נחל רחם (תרגום השם בערבית: ואדי אל רחמא,: Nahal Raham (Arabic name: Wadi al-Rahma, وادي الرحمة) is a wadi in the southern Negev, Israel.
כְּפַר סִירְקִין הוא מושב באזור השרון לי: Kfar Sirkin is a moshav in the Sharon area near Petah Tikva, belonging to the Drom HaSharon Regional Council.
כְּפַר-חֲסִידִים הוא מושב בעמק זבולון לי: Kfar Hasidim is a moshav in the Zevulun Valley near Kiryat Ata and Rekhasim, within the Zevulun Regional Council.
יד קנדי הוא אתר הנצחה לנשיא ארצות הברית: Yad Kennedy is a memorial to US President John F. Kennedy, built in the Aminadav area in the Jerusalem Hills.
הר תמנע (בערבית: جَبَل تمنَع) נמצא בהרי: Mount Timna (Arabic: جَبَل تمنَع) is in the Eilat Mountains, in the southern Arava, about 1.5 km from the entrance to Timna Park.
מרינה הרצליה היא מרינה השוכנת לחופה של ה: Herzliya Marina is a marina on the coast of the city of Herzliya, south of the Dan Accadia Hotel and behind Tel Michal.
נַחַל עַמּוּד הוא נחל באזור הגליל העליון: Nahal Amud is a stream in the Upper Galilee region that flows into the Sea of Galilee. It is the highest of the country's perennial streams.
הר צפחות הוא הר מגמתי בדרומה של ארץ ישרא: Mount Tzfahot is a magmatic mountain in the south of Israel, along the northern part of the Gulf of Eilat, and is the southern tip of the Eilat Mountains ridge.
נחל שחורת הוא נחל קצר, הזורם בעונת החורף: Nahal Shehoret is a short stream that flows in the winter season in the Eilat Mountains area. The stream has a seasonal water source, a water gap and a granite canyon.
תל חליף (במקור: תל חווילפה) הוא תל קדום: Tel Halif (originally Tell Khuweilfeh) is an ancient tell in the northern Negev, about 20 km north-east of Beer Sheva, west of Kibbutz Lahav.
נחל חווה (בערבית: نهر حواء \"נהר חואא\",: Nahal Hava (Arabic: نهر حواء "Nahr Hawa", "Wadi Mashish ash-Shariqa") is an ephemeral stream, one of the tributaries of Nahal Zin in the central Negev Highlands.
נחל קֶדֶשׁ הוא נחל אכזב, מצוקי, ברום של: Nahal Kedesh is an ephemeral, cliff-lined stream at an elevation of about 450 metres that begins in the Lebanon area and ends in the Hula Valley. The lower part of the stream is closed to access.
נַחַל צִבְעוֹן (בערבית: ואדי צוביע; נקרא: Nahal Tzivon (Arabic: Wadi Subei'; also called Nahal Gurei HaArayot – Lion Cubs Stream) is an ephemeral stream located in the Upper Galilee and one of the tributaries of Nahal Dishon.
תל גּוֹדֵד הוא אתר ארכאולוגי באזור שפלת: Tel Goded is an archaeological site in the Judean Shephelah, which includes among other things remains from the biblical period and the Roman period, and hiding complexes from the time of Bar Kokhba.
חבל לכיש הוא גוש התיישבות בדרום, בין הרי: The Lachish Region is a settlement bloc in the south, between the Judean Hills to the east and Ashkelon to the west. At its centre is the city of Kiryat Gat. The region is named after the ancient city of Lachish.
בית אהרנסון הוא ביתה של משפחת אהרנסון במ: The Aaronsohn House is the home of the Aaronsohn family in the moshava of Zikhron Ya'akov, and has housed the NILI Museum since 1956. The house stands at 40 HaMeyasdim Street in Zikhron Ya'akov.
א-נבי יושע (בערבית: النبي يوشع) היה כפר: An-Nabi Yusha (Arabic: النبي يوشع) was a Shia Arab village in the Upper Galilee, with a mausoleum and a Muslim cemetery. Today the locality of Ramot Naftali stands on the site.
נַחַל פּוֹלֵג (בערבית: وادي الفالق; ואדי: Nahal Poleg (Arabic: وادي الفالق; Wadi al-Faliq; the dividing stream) is a stream draining an area in the Sharon region of Israel, flowing into the Mediterranean north of the Wingate Institute in the Netanya area.
הר שחורת הוא חלק מרכס הרי אילת, ונמצא בי: Mount Shehoret is part of the Eilat Mountains ridge, located between Nahal Shehoret and Nahal Roded. It is so named because of the black rocks in its lower part that border Nahal Shehoret, which runs at its foot.
הארבל הוא מצוּק הנמצא בצפון ישראל במזרח: The Arbel is a cliff in northern Israel in the eastern Lower Galilee, north-west of Tiberias and north of the Arbel Valley. Mount Arbel rises to 181 metres above sea level, about 390 metres above the Sea of Galilee.
שַׁחֲרוּת הוא יישוב קהילתי בערבה השייך ל: Shaharut is a community settlement in the Arava belonging to the Hevel Eilot Regional Council, about 37 km north of the city of Eilat. It is located on the edge of the fault escarpment, west of Kibbutz Yotvata, 550 metres above sea level.
נחל עַפְרָן (מערבית: وادي عفران, תעתיק מ: Nahal Afran (from Arabic: وادي عفران, exact transliteration: Wadi Afran) is an ephemeral stream on the southern slopes of the Hatira Ridge in the northern Negev. The stream has a steep canyon channel with waterfalls, rock pools and an impressive gorge.
רָמוֹת נַפְתָּלִי הוא מושב באזור הצפון ל: Ramot Naftali is a moshav in the Northern District near the border between Israel and Lebanon, belonging to the Mevo'ot HaHermon Regional Council. The locality is so named because it is located in the Naftali Hills, within the territory of the tribe of Naftali.
מצפה עופר הוא מצפה יערנים של קק\"ל, השוכ: Mitzpe Ofer is a KKL-JNF foresters' lookout located in the Hof HaCarmel Forest, on the western slopes of the Carmel, between the localities of Kerem Maharal to the east and Tzrufa to the west. The site is named after the nearby Moshav Ofer.
מנזר גְבירתנו של שבעת המכאובים, הידוע יו: The Monastery of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows, better known as Latrun Monastery or the Monastery of the Silent Monks, is a Benedictine-Cistercian-Trappist monastery for men, located in Latrun at the south-eastern end of the Ayalon Valley.
Arad is a city in the Southern District of Israel. The city lies in the Judean Desert, on the Kidod Ridge, at an elevation of about 600 metres above sea level. Its municipal area is 125,610 dunams. Arad was declared a city in 1995.
יער לַהַב הוא יער נטוע בדרום ישראל הממוק: Lahav Forest is a planted forest in southern Israel located between the northern Negev, the southern Judean Shephelah and the southern Hebron Hills, covering about 30,000 dunams. The localities adjacent to it are Dvir, Lahav, Lehavim, Lakiya and Eshkolot.
תל לכיש (בערבית: تل الدوير, תל אֶ-דֻּוֵי: Tel Lachish (Arabic: تل الدوير, Tell ed-Duweir) is a major tell in the Judean Shephelah. It covers about 124 dunams and was identified by the American scholar William Albright in 1926. In 1994 it was declared a national park.
אַלּוֹנִים הוא קיבוץ בצפון עמק יזרעאל, ל: Alonim is a kibbutz in the northern Jezreel Valley, near Kiryat Tiv'on, affiliated with the Kibbutz Movement. The kibbutz, which settled at its present location in 1938, lies within the jurisdiction of the Jezreel Valley Regional Council.
נחל נקרות הוא נחל אכזב באזור מכתש רמון ה: Nahal Nekarot is an ephemeral stream in the Makhtesh Ramon area that flows into Nahal HaArava. In Arabic the stream is called Wadi al-Jarir ("the dragging stream"). It is so named because of the many niches carved by flash floods into the canyon walls.
פארק נחל חדרה הוא פארק שמנוהל על ידי נחל: Nahal Hadera Park is a park managed by Nehalim, the Hadera Tourism Development Company, located in the western part of Nahal Hadera, between Road 2 to the east and the Mediterranean coast to the west, and south of the Orot Rabin power station.
מְצָדָה (מַסָּדָה בכתיב מיושן) הוא מבצר: Masada (Metzada; 'Massada' in older spelling) is an ancient fortress on the summit of an isolated mesa on the eastern edge of the Judean Desert, rising to 63 metres above sea level and about 480 metres above the Dead Sea at its foot.
כעביה-טבאש-חג'אג'רה (בערבית: كعبية، طباش:
Ka'abiyye-Tabbash-Hajajre (Arabic: كعبية، طباش،حجاجرة) is a local council in the Northern District of Israel. It was declared a local council in 1996. 
The locality has a health clinic, a football pitch, a community centre and two mosques.
קִרְיַת שְׁמוֹנָה היא העיר הצפונית ביותר: Kiryat Shmona is the northernmost city in Israel. As the only city in the Galilee Panhandle, located alongside Road 90, Kiryat Shmona serves as a regional centre for the surrounding localities in health services, industry, business services and commerce.
נַחַל דִּישוֹן (בעבר ואדי חינדאג') הוא ה: Nahal Dishon (formerly Wadi Hindaj) is the largest of the streams of the eastern Upper Galilee. It begins on the eastern slopes of Mount Meron, is about 31 km long, and at its end flows into the Jordan River (formerly into Lake Hula), north of the Pkak Bridge.
חורבת עָנִים (במקור: ח'רבת ע'ווין א-תחתא: Horvat Anim (originally Khirbet Ghuwein at-Tahta) is the name of a site in the southern Hebron Hills containing the remains of a biblical and Talmudic settlement, about 20 km north-west of Arad and within Yatir Forest. The site is near the locality of Livne to the south-west.
תֵּל-חָדִיד הוא תל הנמצא מצָפון ליער בן: Tel Hadid is a tell located north of Ben Shemen Forest and Road 443 and south of Nahal Natuf. The tell sits on the first line of hills above the coastal plain in the Ben Shemen area and overlooks all of Gush Dan. The Israel National Trail, section no. 20, passes through Tel Hadid.
מרכז ג'ו אלון הוא מרכז חינוכי ותיירותי ל: The Joe Alon Center is an educational and tourism centre for the study of the land and the Negev, located on the edge of Lahav Forest in the northern Negev, just west of Kibbutz Lahav. The centre is best known for the Museum of Bedouin Culture housed there. The centre is named after the pilot Joe Alon.
עין נטפים (בערבית: ביר אל קטר או עין אל: Ein Netafim (Arabic: Bir al-Qatar or Ein al-Qatar) is a freshwater spring in the Eilat Mountains in the channel of Nahal Netafim near the border with Egypt. The spring is about seven km north of Eilat, near Road 12. It is the only spring that flows year-round in the area near Eilat.
סַנְסַנָּה היא התנחלות דתית במתכונת של י: Sansana is a religious settlement in the form of a community settlement in the Meitarim region on the border of the northern Negev and the Hebron Hills, located mostly east of the Green Line but west of the separation barrier, belonging to the Har Hevron Regional Council, where it is the westernmost locality, and to the Amana movement.
סיירת אגוז (נקראה גם גדוד 483) הוקמה לרא: Sayeret Egoz (also called Battalion 483) was first established in 1956 as the Northern Command's reconnaissance unit on the orders of the Northern Command's commanding general, Yitzhak Rabin, after Israel invaded Sinai during Operation "Kadesh". Its founder and first commander was Aryeh Gardi. The unit was disbanded in 1974.
כפר כַּנָּא (בערבית: كفر كنا) היא מועצה: Kafr Kanna (Arabic: كفر كنا) is an Arab local council in the Lower Galilee, located north of the cities of Nof HaGalil and Nazareth. It was declared a local council in 1968. About 90% of the village's residents are Muslim and the rest Christian. The locality is identified with the ancient settlement of Cana, sacred to Christianity.
אַפּוֹלוֹנְיָה־אַרְסוּף (גם תֵּל אַרְשָׁ: Apollonia-Arsuf (also Tel Arshaf) is an ancient fortress and city whose remains lie on the coastal plain on the kurkar cliffs of the southern Sharon, west of the Nof Yam neighbourhood in Herzliya, near present-day Sidna Ali. The site has been prepared for visitors and a national park was established there.
נַחַל סַעַר (וָאדִי חַשַׁבֶּה) הוא נחל ה:
Nahal Sa'ar (Wadi Hashabeh) is a stream that flows between the northern Golan Heights and the Hermon ridge. The stream is known chiefly for the Sa'ar Waterfall, located near Route 99, and is characterized by an impressive flow after the rains.
The stream empties into Nahal Hermon about 500 meters southwest of the Banias spring.
גבעת האֵם (נקראת בערבית תל אבו חנזיר) הי: Giv'at HaEm (known in Arabic as Tel Abu Hanzir) is a basalt hill 196 meters above sea level located on the slopes of the Golan, at the edge of the Hula Valley. Like Kfar Szold, which lies about a kilometer and a half to the south, the hill is also named after Henrietta Szold, who was called the "Mother of Youth Aliyah".
עֵינַת הוא קיבוץ באזור השרון השייך למועצ: Einat is a kibbutz in the Sharon region belonging to the Drom HaSharon Regional Council. It lies southwest of Rosh HaAyin, and the only access road to it branches off Route 444, which connects Rosh HaAyin with Petah Tikva. In addition, the route of Highway 6 passes a few dozen meters west of the kibbutz, but does not lead to it.
נמל תל אביב הוא נמל על חוף הים התיכון שפ: The Tel Aviv Port is a port on the Mediterranean coast that operated at the mouth of the Yarkon River in northwestern Tel Aviv-Yafo in the years 1938–1965 and was called "the first Hebrew port". The establishment of the port was considered a significant step in the development of Hebrew shipping during the Mandate period. Since the first decade of the 21st century, the port compound has served as a leisure and entertainment complex.
נחל גוברין הוא נחל אכזב בשפלת יהודה, שרא:
Nahal Guvrin is an ephemeral stream in the Judean Lowlands (Shephelah), which begins in the Hebron Hills and ends at Nahal Lachish. The stream flows in a general northwesterly direction.
The stream drains an area of about 204 km², from the Hebron Hills (the area of the villages of Dura and Tapuah) at an elevation of about 850 meters above sea level, down to its confluence with Nahal Lachish after about 48 km.
מצפה מודיעין הוא מגדל תצפית שריפות ביער: Mitzpe Modi'in is a fire lookout tower in the Ben Shemen Forest, one of 42 fire lookout towers erected in the forests of the Jewish National Fund (KKL). They were intended to serve as observation posts for warning of and protection against fires. Since the late 1990s, in light of technological developments in detecting fire outbreaks, the towers are mostly unmanned.
מִדּרֶשֶׁת בֶּן-גּוּרִיּוֹן היא יישוב קה: Midreshet Ben-Gurion is a community settlement in Sde Zin in the Ramat HaNegev region, near Kibbutz Sde Boker, between Beersheba and Mitzpe Ramon. It includes a number of educational and research institutions. Most of the settlement's activity is operated by the Midreshet Sde Boker corporation; alongside Midreshet Ben-Gurion lies the "Ben-Gurion's Tomb National Park".
יער מיתר הוא יער נטוע בדרום ישראל, המקיף: Meitar Forest is a planted forest in southern Israel surrounding the town of Meitar to the north and east. The forest covers an area of about 8,200 dunams and lies at an elevation of about 450 m above sea level. It is a central component of the region's ecological and scenic landscape, contributing to the quality of life of the area's residents and serving as a recreation and leisure site.
כְּפַר גִּלְעָדִי הוא קיבוץ באצבע הגליל: Kfar Giladi is a kibbutz in the Galilee Panhandle near Metula and Kiryat Shmona, belonging to the Upper Galilee Regional Council. The kibbutz was formed as a result of a merger carried out in the 1920s and 1930s between Kfar Giladi, Tel Hai and Kibbutz Tiberias. South of the kibbutz (within the bounds of the former Tel Hai) now stands the Kiryat Shmona University in the Galilee.
זִכְרוֹן יַעֲקֹב היא מועצה מקומית במחוז:
Zichron Ya'akov is a local council in the Haifa District of Israel. It was founded as a moshava on 6 December 1882 by Hovevei Zion immigrants from Romania, and was the second moshava of the First Aliyah (after Rishon LeZion).
The moshava sits on Hotem HaCarmel, the southern part of the Carmel ridge. It was declared a local council in 1950.
גן לאומי ירקון הוא גן לאומי המשלב כיום ש: Yarkon National Park is a national park that today combines two sites: one is Tel Afek, entered from Route 483, between Petah Tikva and Rosh HaAyin, and the other is the sources of the Yarkon River, accessed from Route 5 or Route 40, via the entrance to the Baptist Village. The park has sites to visit alongside expanses of lawn, trees and water, for recreation and leisure.
יער יתיר הוא יער נטוע הנמצא בחבל יתיר, כ: Yatir Forest is a planted forest located in the Yatir region, about 30 km northeast of Beersheba. Its planted area extends over 37,000 dunams. It is the largest planted forest in Israel, and according to KKL-JNF the largest man-made forest in the world planted in a semi-arid region. It is bordered on the east by the communities of Har Amasa and Beit Yatir, and on the north by Livne (Shani) and Asa'el.
מִכְמוֹרֶת הוא מושב בעמק חפר, כ-2 ק\"מ מ:
Michmoret is a moshav in the Hefer Valley, about 2 km south of Hadera and about 6 km north of Netanya. It is part of the Emek Hefer Regional Council, and is the northernmost settlement in it.
The moshav is adjacent to the mouth of Nahal Alexander on the Mediterranean coast. Next to the moshav is a bay that once served as an ancient harbor, and the Ramot Yam secondary school within the Mevo'ot Yam youth village.
פארק עֲדֻלָּם, או בשמו המלא פארק מערות ע:
Adullam Park, or by its full name Adullam Caves Park, is a park in the eastern Judean Lowlands in the Adullam region, containing archaeological remains from various periods. The park is named after the biblical city of Adullam, mentioned in the Bible, which is identified with a tel located within the park.
Development of the park began after the completion of the separation barrier east of the park, toward the Hebron Hills.
שער הַגַּיְא (בערבית: باب الواد – בָּאב: Sha'ar HaGai (Arabic: باب الواد – Bab al-Wad) is a narrow entrance passage from the lowlands into the Jerusalem Hills, located today on Highway 1, at the 35th kilometer from Tel Aviv. Nearby is the Sha'ar HaGai Interchange. From Sha'ar HaGai, Highway 1 continues eastward toward Jerusalem for about six kilometers through a narrow valley along the bed of Nahal Nahshon (Wadi Ali) as far as the Sho'eva area.
נַחַל פְּרָצִים הוא נחל אכזב בדרום מדבר: Nahal Peratzim is an ephemeral stream in the southern Judean Desert. Nahal Peratzim originates in the Amiaz Plain, which it drains; it flows northeast, is 5.5 km long, and at its end joins the drainage basin of Nahal Heimar and Nahal Zohar, emptying into the Zohar Valley and the Dead Sea north of Mount Sodom. The stream's gorge reaches a depth of about 50 meters and is only a few meters wide.
גני רמת הנדיב הוא פארק טבע רחב-ידיים, שה: Ramat HaNadiv Gardens is an expansive nature park established around the burial plot of Baron Benjamin Edmond de Rothschild, south of Zichron Ya'akov. The site is dedicated to Baron Rothschild in recognition of his great contribution to the Jewish people. Rothschild died in 1934. In the early 1950s his remains were brought for burial at Ramat HaNadiv, and the park (which had existed before then) was dedicated to his memory.
נְאוֹת סְמָדַר הוא קיבוץ בדרום הערבה סמו: Neot Semadar is a kibbutz in the southern Arava near the Shizafon Junction, on Route 40, belonging to the Hevel Eilot Regional Council. The kibbutz is a member of the TAKAM (United Kibbutz Movement). The kibbutz was founded as the "Shizafon" Nahal outpost in 1980, and after it failed to get off the ground, the Neot Semadar group settled there in 1989 and established a community centered on ecological and organic themes. The settlement extends over an area of about 800 dunams.
נַחַל אֲלֶכְּסַנְדֶּר (בעבר: נהר אסְכַּנ: Nahal Alexander (formerly: the Iskanderuna River) is a stream that flows from the Samarian Hills to the Mediterranean Sea. For most of its course it flows through the Hefer Valley. The stream's mouth lies north of Netanya, between the moshavim of Michmoret and Beit Yanai. The stream drains the Nablus area and central Samaria, as well as part of the Sharon. The stream is about 32 km long. The lower part of the stream and its surroundings are a declared national park.
עין סהרונים הוא מעיין קטן, היחיד במכתש ר:
Ein Saharonim is a small spring, the only one in Makhtesh Ramon, and the largest and most important source of water in the makhtesh. The spring is located in the Mezuke Zinim (Zin Cliffs) Nature Reserve, near Metzad Saharonim – an ancient way station.
The name Ein Saharonim derives from the drooping saharon (acacia mistletoe) plant that grows in the area. In Arabic the spring is called al-Mahla ("the dry spring", "the spring of drought"), like the Nabataean khan Qasr al-Mahla.
נחל חווארים הוא נחל אכזב בנגב המרכזי, דר:
Nahal Havarim is an ephemeral stream in the central Negev, south of Midreshet Ben-Gurion and north of the town of Mitzpe Ramon. It begins at Route 40 near Tziporim Junction and ends at the foot of Ma'ale HaGar, where it joins Nahal Avdat and together with it forms Nahal Zin. Nahal Karkash connects to Nahal Havarim roughly at its midpoint.
Nahal Havarim enters the Zin Valley, which lies between the Avdat Plateau and Ramat HaNegev.
עין עקב הוא שמם של שני מעיינות הבוקעים ע: Ein Akev is the name of two springs that emerge along the channel of Nahal Akev on the Avdat Plateau in the central Negev, southeast of the community settlement of Midreshet Ben-Gurion and near Nahal Zin and Ein Avdat. The name derives from the Arabic name of the place, Ein Umm Ka'b, meaning "spring of the heel". The stone after which the spring is named is a black flint rock found at Upper Ein Akev, which stands out sharply from its white surroundings.
מִצְפֵּה רָמוֹן היא מועצה מקומית במחוז ה:
Mitzpe Ramon is a local council in the Southern District of Israel.
Mitzpe Ramon lies in the center of the Negev Highlands, on the northern rim of Makhtesh Ramon, about 80 km south of Beersheba and about 150 km north of Eilat. Its jurisdiction covers 64,500 dunams and it has about 5,047 residents. It was founded in 1953 as a work camp for the laborers who paved the road to Eilat, and became a permanent settlement in 1956.
מוֹאָב הוא שמו של חבל ארץ בעבר הירדן המז:
Moab is the name of a region in eastern Transjordan during the Israelite period, corresponding largely to the Iron Age, from the end of the 2nd millennium BCE to the 6th century BCE. According to the sources, Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, between the Dead Sea escarpment and the Arabian Desert, within the territory of the present-day Kingdom of Jordan.
Moab is a predominantly mountainous land, and the mountains between Nahal Zered and Nahal Arnon are called the Mountains of Moab.
בקעת תִּמְנָע היא בקעה בשוליים המערביים: The Timna Valley is a valley on the western margins of the southern Arava, about 25 kilometers north of Eilat. The horseshoe-shaped valley extends over an area of about 60 square kilometers and is bounded by steep cliffs on three sides. It is drained by Nahal Timna in the north and Nahal Nehushtan in the south, which flow to the Arava east of it. At its center rises Mount Timna to a height of 453 meters. The area has an extreme desert climate.
שמורת נחל הבניאס או שמורת נחל חרמון היא: The Nahal Banias Nature Reserve, or Nahal Hermon Nature Reserve, is a nature reserve located at the foot of Mount Hermon, at the meeting point between the Golan Heights and the Hula Valley, near the community of Snir. It extends along Nahal Hermon from the area of the Banias springs down to the head of the sources of the Jordan. The reserve was declared in 1977 over an area of about 800 dunams. In 2009 the reserve was expanded and a further 500 dunams or so were added upstream, and since then the reserve's area has stood at about 1,300 dunams.
קרני חיטין הוא שמו של הר געש כבוי בגליל:
The Horns of Hattin (Karnei Hittin) is the name of an extinct volcano in the Lower Galilee, near Mount Arbel; its maximum height is 326 meters, and it lies about 5 km west of Tiberias, above the city. The mountain owes its name to its two peaks, which are shaped like horns. It is thought that its two peaks – known as the "horns" – are volcanic plugs exposed by erosion. In 2007 the area around the mountain was declared a national park.
From the Horns of Hattin one can see the Sea of Galilee (Kinneret), Gilead, the Golan and the Galilee.
עֵין בּוֹקֵק הוא מתחם התיירות והבילוי הע: Ein Bokek is the main tourism and leisure complex on the Israeli side of the Dead Sea. The complex lies within the Tamar Regional Council, on the shores of Pond 5 in the southern basin of the lake, at 392 meters below sea level. The Ein Bokek hotels were built on the alluvial fan of Nahal Zohar, between the lakeshore to the east and Route 90 to the west, and the site is about a kilometer and a half long from north to south. The place is named after the Ein Bokek springs in Nahal Bokek.
המכתש הקטן (בשמו המדויק: מכתש חֲצֵרָה) ה:
The Small Crater (HaMakhtesh HaKatan; by its precise name, Makhtesh Hatzera) is an erosional crater, the third largest of the five makhteshim of the Negev and the Sinai Peninsula.
The Small Crater is located in the Hatzera ridge and is therefore also called Makhtesh Hatzera (Arabic: الخضيرة – al-Khudayra – "the threshing floor of the palms"). It is the easternmost makhtesh in the series of craters formed in the anticlines of the Negev Highlands and northern Sinai, which include Makhtesh Ramon, the Large Crater (HaMakhtesh HaGadol) and the Arif makhteshim.
In June 2019 the state declared the crater a nature reserve.
הר עמשא הוא הר בהרי חברון, מדרום ליישוב:
Har Amasa (Mount Amasa) is a mountain in the Hebron Hills, south of the community of Har Amasa and 13 km north of Arad. The mountain is 859 meters above sea level, and from its summit one can look out over the southern Judean Desert and the Arad Valley, the northern Negev Highlands and, to the north, the Hebron Hills. 
The mountain lies within the jurisdiction of the Tamar Regional Council, and around it is a declared nature reserve, the "Har Amasa Nature Reserve". The mountain received its name in modern times after Amasa son of Jether, who was commander of Absalom's army and later commander of King David's army.
מקום קברו של רבי שמעון בר יוחאי (רשב\"י): The burial place of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (Rashbi), a Tanna of the 2nd century, lies according to the Midrash in ancient Meron. Today, the tomb on Mount Meron is regarded as a matter of Jewish consensus and is among the most famous in the Land of Israel and the world, and the second most visited religious site in the country by annual number of visitors, after the Western Wall. The hillula held at the site every year on Lag BaOmer is the largest annual civil-religious event in Israel. A common custom is to perform the chalakah there, the ceremony of a boy's first haircut at the age of three.
שבלול החרמון (שם מדעי: Helix pachya, בעב: The Hermon snail (scientific name: Helix pachya, formerly Helix texta) is a snail of the family Helicidae and the order of air-breathing land snails (pulmonates) that lives on land. The Hermon snail is a species endemic to the Land of Israel and is found only on the slopes of Mount Hermon, mainly in the Nahal Hermon Nature Reserve. In the past the Hermon snail was classified under the species Helix texta, but after re-examination it became clear that it is the same species as Helix pachya, and it was therefore reclassified under that name, since the species Helix pachya had been described first.
Hod Akev is a residual hill (inselberg) located at the Zin Cliffs (Mezuke Zinim). The mountain is conical in shape, and its height is about 576 meters above sea level. The mountain is part of the Avdat Plateau.

The mountain takes its name from the nearby Nahal Akev and Ein Akev; the name derives from the Arabic word ka'b (كَعْب).
From the summit there is a wide view over Nahal Akev, Ramat Boker and the Zin Valley. The ascent of the mountain on its northern side along the Israel National Trail is extremely steep, and includes climbing with the aid of iron rungs.
In the past several hikers were killed climbing the cliff.
מקדש הנמרים הוא אתר ארכאולוגי, בו התגלה: The Leopards Temple is an archaeological site where an open-air temple that served as a prehistoric cult site was discovered. The site lies east of the access road to the community of Shaharut, northeast of Ovda Airport in the Ovda Valley. The place is one of some 160 open-air temples discovered so far in the Negev and eastern Sinai, and it was in use for about 4,000 years, from the middle of the 6th millennium BCE (the Late Neolithic period) until the first half of the 2nd millennium BCE (the Middle Bronze Age).
עמודי שלמה הם צורות סלע, הנראות למתבונן:
Solomon's Pillars are rock formations that appear to the viewer as giant stone columns. The pillars are located in the Timna Valley, north of Eilat. The pillars were formed by weathering caused by wind and water along fault lines in the red sandstone. Solomon's Pillars rise to a height of about 40 meters.
The impressive shape of the pillars, which look like the columns of a temple, led the ancient Egyptians who mined copper in the valley to build at their foot a temple to Hathor, the goddess of the mines, a temple that was later also used by the Midianites.
נַחַל צֶאֱלִים (בערבית: وادِي السيّال- ו: Nahal Tze'elim (Arabic: وادِي السيّال – Wadi as-Sayyal) is one of the largest ephemeral streams among the Judean Desert streams descending to the Dead Sea; its length from its source to its mouth is about 32 km. The stream's drainage basin covers about 287 km². The stream drains the southeastern Hebron Hills near the community of Ma'on, continues north of Arad and empties into the Dead Sea north of Masada. In addition to many water pools (gevim), which fill each year after the winter rain floods, four springs emerge in the stream.
נַחַל גִּשְׁרוֹן (בערבית: وادِي جسرية –:
Nahal Gishron (Arabic: وادِي جسرية – Wadi Jasriya) is an ephemeral stream in the Eilat Mountains. 
Its upper tributaries begin in the area of Ras an-Naqab near the Netafim Crossing. The stream descends steeply to its mouth at the Red Sea in Taba, Egypt. 
The stream has hiking trails along its upper sections, from which there are views of its landscapes. The stream has several cliffs where rappelling can be done.
The final section of the Israel National Trail begins in the stream, ending at the Eilat Field School at the foot of Mount Tzfahot.
לטרון הוא רכס בעמק איילון, במרחק של כ-15:
Latrun is a ridge in the Ayalon Valley, about 15 kilometers west of the city of Jerusalem. The ridge commands the road to Jerusalem, is considered an important strategic objective, and major battles were fought there, from biblical times to the Six-Day War.
The name originates in a corruption of the name of the Latrun fortress, a Crusader castle built on the site that was called in French "Le toron des chevaliers" ("the tower of the knights" in free translation). According to another hypothesis, the name derives from the Latin Castellum bonu Latronis, the castle of the good thief.
אמות המים של קיסריה היא מערכת של אמות מי: The aqueducts of Caesarea are a system of aqueducts that carried water to the city of Caesarea in antiquity. The aqueducts of Caesarea functioned throughout the city's existence – from its founding in the days of Herod until the 13th century, when it was destroyed in the days of the Mamluk sultan Baybars. Although Caesarea was built over a high water table, which allowed water supply by means of wells, the city's builders provided a supply of running water to the city, as was customary in the great cities of the Roman period. The system was composed of several different parts.
כביש הנפט (באנגלית: Petroleum Road, מכונ: The Petroleum Road (Kvish HaNeft; also known as the Oil Route) is a rutted, privately owned longitudinal asphalt road in the Golan Heights, 47 km long, extending from the Syrian border near Mount Peres in the eastern central Golan to the Lebanese border, near the village of Ghajar. The road takes its name from the "Trans-Arabian Pipeline" (Trans-Arabian Pipeline Company, the Tapline), along which it was built. This road is a small part of a continuous route that accompanies the oil pipeline along its entire length.
חוּרבַת חָנוֹת (בערבית: ח'רבת אל-ח'אן) ה: Horvat Hanot (Arabic: Khirbet al-Khan) is a ruin on the slopes of the Jerusalem Hills toward the transition to the Judean Lowlands, about a kilometer west of Moshav Mata. The ruin was a wayfarers' inn (khan) from the Mamluk period; the inn served travelers on the Caesar's Road (Derech HaKeisar), which was part of the Roman road from Jerusalem and Bethlehem to the lowlands and Beit Guvrin, and it ceased to function during the Ottoman period in the Land of Israel. At the site are a colorful mosaic floor of a Byzantine-period church, a winepress and a storage pool.
מבצר נמרוד (ידוע גם בשמות קַלְעַת נַמרוּ: Nimrod Fortress (also known as Qal'at Namrud and Qal'at as-Subeiba – Arabic: قلعة الصبيبة) is an archaeological site from the Hellenistic period and the Middle Ages, containing the remains of a large fortress built over the years by Ayyubid and Mamluk armies. The fortress sits at the top of a narrow ridge at an elevation of about 800 meters above sea level, at the foot of Mount Hermon, about 3 kilometers southwest of the community of Neve Ativ and about 1,300 meters northeast of a tributary of Nahal Sa'ar. The site is a declared national park.
מצודת כ\"ח (שמה נֶהֱגֶה \"מצודת כוח\"; נ:
Metzudat Koach (its name, written with the Hebrew letters for 28, is pronounced "Metzudat Koach"; it is also called "Metzudat Yesha" and "Nabi Yusha", after the ruins of the nearby Arab village of Nabi Yusha) is a Tegart fort in the Northern District, about 10 km south of Kiryat Shmona. The fort is named after the 28 fighters killed in its capture during the War of Independence.
The fort today serves as a Border Police base, and beside it stand a memorial and a mass grave in which 19 of those who fell in the battles at the site are buried. In early 2014 the Re'ut (Comradeship) Museum, commemorating the battles and those who fell there, was opened next to the fort.
מְצַד זוֹהַר הוא שמם של שני מבנים עתיקים: Metzad Zohar is the name of two ancient structures in Nahal Zohar, west of Route 90. The eastern structure is the "Israelite" Metzad Zohar, located near the stream's outlet to the Dead Sea. This structure was identified by the archaeologists Yohanan Aharoni and Beno Rothenberg in 1957, and was dated by them to the Iron Age. In 2025, excavations were conducted at the site and the finds are attributed to the Seleucid period. The western structure is located on a cliff rising above the stream, and is called the "Roman" Metzad Zohar, but it is dated to the Crusader and Mamluk periods.
בקעת עוּבדה היא בקעה חולית מוקפת גבעות ב: The Ovda Valley is a sandy valley surrounded by hills in the southern Negev. The valley and the nearby Ovda Cliffs are named after Operation Uvda, which took place in 1949 toward the end of the War of Independence and in the course of which, among other things, its territory was captured. Together with the Sayarim Valley, the valley is one of the two valleys through which the main sections of Nahal Hiyyon pass. The valley is bounded on the south by the Sayarim Valley and on the north by the Timna Cliffs and the northern part of Mount Berech, on the east by Mount Shaharut, Mount Grofit and Mount Argaman, on the north by Mount Shahrur and Mount Perut, and on the west by the Ovda Cliffs.
שְׂדֵה נְחֶמְיָה הוא קיבוץ באצבע הגליל ב:
Sde Nehemia is a kibbutz in the Galilee Panhandle in the northern Hula Valley, about 5 km east of Kiryat Shmona, belonging to the Upper Galilee Regional Council.
The kibbutz was founded in 1940 by immigrants from Austria, Czechoslovakia and the Netherlands (who belonged to the Maccabi HaTza'ir youth movement), on land purchased from the Arab village of ad-Dawwara.
The kibbutz is named after Nehemia de Lieme, a Dutch Zionist activist who was chairman of the Dutch Zionist Federation in 1912–1918 and chairman of the KKL (Jewish National Fund) in 1919–1922.
תל חי הייתה חווה חקלאית קטנה באצבע הגליל: Tel Hai was a small agricultural farm in the Galilee Panhandle at the beginning of the period of Zionist settlement in the Land of Israel. On 1 March 1920 (11 Adar 5680), a battle took place there that became a symbol of the few fighting against the many and of the value of settlement as part of the Zionist ethos. Six Jews were killed in the battle, among them Joseph Trumpeldor. The farm, which became Kibbutz Tel Hai, was merged in 1926 with Kfar Giladi, and its members moved there. On the grounds of the courtyard, a memorial site, Tel-Hai Academic College, the Tel Hai Technological College, an industrial park and a youth hostel were established.
נַחַל יָגוּר הוא נחל אכזב הזורם במורדות: Nahal Yagur is an ephemeral stream flowing down the eastern slopes of Mount Carmel in the High Carmel and passing through "Ashdot Yagur Park", which is part of the Carmel Park. It is also called Wadi Shumariya after the fennel (shumar) bushes that grow in the area. The stream begins in the Isfiya area. It flows southeast of Nahal Ma'apilim toward the Zevulun Valley and empties into the Kishon River. On its way the stream passes through Kibbutz Yagur. Like the other Carmel streams flowing east of the mountain's watershed line, the stream is short, canyon-like and steep-banked. The stream is about 2 km long.
מאובן הוא שריד, תבנית או עקבות של בעל חי:
A fossil is the remains, impression or trace of an animal, plant or other organism from a past geological period that has been preserved in a petrified state. The field of science that studies fossils is paleontology.
The term fossil is usually reserved for remains older than 10,000 years, from before the end of the last ice age. (Later remains may be called subfossils.) Fossils provide important evidence for the precise dating of rock strata, and have supplied much of the information on which the current subdivisions of the geological time scale are based.
נַחַל תָּבוֹר (בערבית: ואדי אל־בִּירָה): Nahal Tavor (Arabic: Wadi al-Bira) is a perennial stream in the Lower Galilee, which originates in the area of Mount Ksulot in the Nazareth Hills, flows southeast and empties into the Jordan River near Tel Shoshan and near Kibbutz Gesher, about 3 km south of Naharayim. On its way it skirts Mount Tabor and drains many tributaries into itself, the main one being Nahal HaShiv'a. The stream forms a geographical boundary between the Sirin Plateau and the Kochav Plateau. In the lower section of the stream, included within the "Nahal Tavor" Nature Reserve, three springs emerge: Ein Rechesh, Ein Ze'ev and Ein Shahal.
נַחַל אֶשְׁתְּמֹעַ הוא נחל אכזב שראשיתו:
Nahal Eshtemoa is an ephemeral stream that begins in the southern Hebron Hills, at an elevation of about 800 meters above sea level, and ends at its confluence with Nahal Yatir, one of the tributaries of Nahal Be'er Sheva, near Hura.
The stream's name derives from the name of the biblical and Talmudic town of Eshtemoa, which is identified with the village of as-Samu, where the stream begins.
The stream's channel runs southwest; at its start it passes at the foot of the community of Shim'a, and further on at the foot of Mount Hiran and alongside the community of Meitar and the route of the Israel National Trail, and it includes several water pools (gevim); in addition, the Israel National Trail passes through the stream.
רכס רמים (מכונה גם בשם \"רכס מנרה\") הוא: The Ramim Ridge (also called the "Manara Ridge") is the central ridge of the Naftali Mountains in the Upper Galilee. The ridge, which runs north–south, lies within the territories of both Lebanon and Israel, and the border line between them passes through it. The ridge's eastern slope descends steeply toward the Hula Valley with an elevation difference of 750 meters over only about two kilometers, while the western slope descends gently toward Nahal Duba in Lebanese territory. Mount Shenan, rising to a height of 902 meters above sea level, is the ridge's summit. The Ramim Ridge is located north of the plateau area known as Ramot Naftali.
שְׁמוּרַת חַי-בָּר כַּרְמֶל הוא מוסד זוא:
The Hai-Bar Carmel Nature Reserve is a zoological institution of the hai-bar (wildlife reserve) type founded by the Nature Reserves Authority with the aim of protecting, and reintroducing to the wild, animals that once lived in northern Israel. Hai-Bar Carmel is located in the Carmel mountains in northern Israel, and it is the Mediterranean-climate counterpart of Hai-Bar Yotvata in the Arava.
In 1973 fencing began of a reserve area for Hai-Bar Carmel in the Nahal Galim basin. The Hai-Bar Carmel Reserve extends over an area of about 6,000 dunams. From Hai-Bar Carmel, the Persian fallow deer and the roe deer, which had disappeared from the country's landscape, have been released into the wild.
The institution's director is the zoologist Ben Rosenberg.
מכתש רמון הוא מכתש הסחיפה הגדול בעולם. ה:
Makhtesh Ramon is the largest erosion crater (makhtesh) in the world. It is located in Israel and is one of the five makhteshim of the Negev, and an International Dark Sky Reserve. The landscape of Makhtesh Ramon is unique. On the northern rim of the makhtesh lies the town of Mitzpe Ramon.
The makhtesh is about 40 km long, up to about 9 km wide and up to about 350 meters deep. In the east, the makhtesh is divided by Mount Ardon into two valleys: the Ardon Valley and the Mahmal Valley. Most of the makhtesh's area is drained by Nahal Ramon, which is called in Arabic "Wadi ar-Ruman", possibly because Romans passed through this area, on the Incense Route.
חולות כסוי הוא שטח המכוסה בחולות נודדים:
The Kasuy Sands (Holot Kasuy) are an area covered by shifting sand dunes located in the eastern Ovda Valley in the southern Negev, about a kilometer northeast of the Ovda base, about 5 km southwest of Mount Ayit and about 6 km north of the community of Shaharut. Together with the Samar Sands in the Arava, these are the only dunes in the Negev between Makhtesh Ramon and the Negev Highlands and Eilat.
The Israel National Trail passes through the dune area, where Mount Perut rises; north of the dunes runs Nahal Kasuy and to the south Nahal Yitro. The Kasuy Sands were formed by the drift of soft, light sand carried by strong winds and accumulated on these dunes, as in the Samar Sands.
דבורייה (בערבית: دبورية / دبوریه) היא מו:
Daburiyya (Arabic: دبورية / دبوریه) is a local council in the Northern District of Israel, located on the edge of the Jezreel Valley at the foot of Mount Tabor. The village of Daburiyya was declared a local council in 1961. According to the Central Bureau of Statistics, as of the end of 2022, all the residents of Daburiyya were Muslim Arabs.
Daburiyya is built on the slope of Mount Tabor, at its junction with the adjacent plain of the Ksulot Valley. Its form of construction is mainly rural, but it also has residential buildings and structures of one to four stories. The current head of the Daburiyya council is Rif'at Azaiza.
הַר תָּבוֹר הוא הר בגליל התחתון, מדרום ל:
Mount Tabor is a mountain in the Lower Galilee, south of the Nazareth Hills ridge and north of the Jezreel Valley. Its summit is 562 meters above sea level, and about 400 meters above its surroundings. The summit is prominent and visible from afar throughout the Galilee and even from the Golan Heights. Viewed from Kfar Tavor, from east to west, the summit appears pointed. Viewed from south to north, from the direction of Afula, the summit appears rounded and gentle.
On the mountain's slopes lie three communities: Umm al-Ghanam (at the southeastern end), Daburiyya (at the bottom of the western slope) and Shibli (at the bottom of the eastern slope), and east of it the moshava of Kfar Tavor.
יקבי כרמל (לשעבר \"כרמל מזרחי\", וקודם ל: Carmel Winery (formerly "Carmel Mizrahi", and before that "Carmel") is an Israeli wine-producing company that operates several wineries in Israel. Its first two wineries were established in 1889 in the moshavot of Rishon LeZion and Zichron Ya'akov by Baron Benjamin Edmond de Rothschild, and they are still active today. The company's logo depicts the spies sent by Moses to scout the land, who returned with a cluster of grapes "and they bore it between two upon a staff" (Numbers 13:23). The logo was originally purchased from the Efrat Winery, and the image was later also adopted by the Ministry of Tourism as the official symbol of Israeli tourism.
נחל צָפִית (בערבית: ואדי אלמֻראקאבּ) הוא:
Nahal Tzafit (Arabic: Wadi al-Muraqqab) is a stream channel in the northern Hatzera ridge near Metzad Tamar and Ma'ale Tamar, south of the Dead Sea. It is about 25 kilometers long. The stream's channel begins west of Mount Hatzera, descending at first northward and then eastward to the northern Arava. In its upper part the Ein Tzafit spring emerges. The stream descends over a high waterfall and several lower waterfalls to its lower section, as far as its outlet into Nahal Zin.
Until 1956 the stream was known by its Arabic name. That year the Government Names Committee set the name "Nahal Tzafit".
In April 1975 the stream was polluted by effluent that flowed from the Dead Sea Periclase plant.
סטף (בערבית: صطاف, בתעתיק לעברית: צטאף):
Sataf (Arabic: صطاف, transliterated into Hebrew as Tzataf) was an Arab village in the Jerusalem Hills on the eastern slope of Mount Eitan descending to Nahal Sorek, about ten kilometers west of Jerusalem. During the War of Independence the village was captured as part of Operation Dani, and its inhabitants left and were not permitted to return after the war.
The site lies about a kilometer northwest of Moshav Even Sapir, and preserves and reconstructs traditional and ancient hill agriculture that still exists in villages such as Battir and Wadi Fukin in the Judean Hills. Irrigated agriculture at the site was sustained mainly by the waters of two perched springs, Ein Sataf (Ein al-Balad) and Ein Bikura (Ein ash-Sharqiya).
עמק ססגון שוכן בצפון מזרח בקעת תמנע, כ-2: The Sasgon Valley lies in the northeastern Timna Valley, about 25 km north of Eilat and about 3 km west of Route 90, and west of Kibbutz Elifaz. Around the valley stand residual hills of Nubian sandstone, and the Israel National Trail passes through its heart. The valley lies outside the boundaries of Timna Park and is open to the public free of charge. From 2007 and for about a dozen years, a public struggle was waged against the construction of a hotel complex inside the valley. The struggle was crowned with success, and in December 2019 the National Planning and Building Council unanimously approved a plan under which the Sasgon Valley will be declared a nature reserve. Under this plan, the construction of a hotel will be permitted near the entrance to Timna Park.
אִירוּס נַצְרָתִי או אִירִיס נַצְרָתִי (: The Nazareth iris (Hebrew: Irus Natzrati or Iris Natzrati; scientific name: Iris bismarckiana) is a species in the Oncocyclus section (the royal irises), in the subgenus Iris of the genus Iris. The Nazareth iris is endemic to northern Israel, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria. In Israel the species grows in the Nazareth Hills, on Givat HaMoreh, in the Naftali Hills and at the foot of Mount Hermon. East of the Jordan River, the Nazareth iris grows in the Gilead region of Jordan. Because Muslims customarily plant it in cemeteries, it is assumed that certain populations were brought to their locations by humans. Several populations growing in the wild probably developed from plants that were planted in Muslim cemeteries.
נבי חזורי (בערבית: مقام النبي الحزوري, م:
Nabi Hazuri (Arabic: مقام النبي الحزوري, مقام سيّدنا الحزّوري, مقام الحزوري) is the burial site of the Druze holy man Sheikh Othman Hazuri, located in the northern Golan Heights about a kilometer east of Nimrod Fortress (Qal'at Namrud). At the site is an ancient oak grove, which became sanctified following the sanctity of the tomb. The tomb structure from the period of Syrian rule had a white cone-shaped dome. In recent decades the structure has been expanded.
The site also holds a memorial to the fallen of the Egoz reconnaissance unit in its various incarnations, with thirty-one memorial corners in memory of the unit's thirty-one fallen. Also commemorated at the site is Nachman Alexandron, one of the heads of the Jewish National Fund, who planned the site before his death.
נחל מירון הוא אחד מיובליו של נחל עמוד, ה:
Nahal Meron is one of the tributaries of Nahal Amud, located in the Upper Galilee. The stream flows eastward from the slopes of Mount Meron, passing through agricultural land and many natural areas, and empties into Nahal Amud. The stream is about 5 kilometers long and is considered relatively short, but of great historical and geographical importance. The stream's course passes near Moshav Meron and north of Har Mesarvim. Along it are several springs, including Ein Meron ("Mei Megiddo") and Ein Bar-Yochai.
Up on the northern bank, near Moshav Meron, are the ancient synagogue of Meron and the tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. On the southern bank are the remains of the synagogue at Horvat Shema.
נַחַל תַּנִּינִים (בערבית: وَادِي ٱلزَّر:
Nahal Taninim (Arabic: وَادِي ٱلزَّرْقَاءِ - Wadi az-Zarqa, "the Blue Stream") is a perennial stream that begins in the Menashe Heights (Ramot Menashe) between the kibbutzim Dalia and Ein HaShofet. The stream flows southwest and empties into the Mediterranean Sea right beside Jisr az-Zarqa and south of Kibbutz Ma'agan Michael. Other, older names for the stream are "Crocodilon" and "Tamasih".
Near Moshav Aviel, the Mekorot water company built a dam across the channel of Nahal Taninim as part of the "Menashe Streams" project. On winter days when the flow in the stream is strong, the stream's water (together with water from the Ada, Barkan and Mishmarot streams) is diverted into a canal that carries the water to an infiltration reservoir for groundwater recharge in the Caesarea dunes.
עמק האלה הוא עמק קטן בשפלת יהודה, מדרום:
The Elah Valley (Emek HaEla) is a small valley in the Judean Lowlands (Shephelah), south of Beit Shemesh, known as the site of the battle between David and Goliath as recounted in the Bible. The Elah Valley is considered one of the most fertile areas in the Land of Israel, and it links the Shephelah with the Judean Hills and the Adullam region, hence its importance over the years. To this day a large number of archaeological sites and biblical tells stand out in the valley and its surroundings.
At the beginning of 2014 a plan to declare the Elah Valley a national park was deposited, and in July 2019 it was declared a national park and passed to the management of the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, mainly because of its historical importance and the desire to limit the southward expansion of Beit Shemesh's urban area into the valley.
דרך נוף יער בית קשת היא דרך נופית בגליל:
The Beit Keshet Forest Scenic Road is a scenic road in the Lower Galilee. It is named after Kibbutz Beit Keshet, which the road passes beside. The northern entrance to the road is next to Camp Shimshon; the entrance is from Route 77, about 2 km west of the Golani Interchange. The road passes by Beit Keshet, next to which is the eastern entrance, reached from Route 65. From there the road turns southwest toward Nof HaGalil.
The southern entrance to the road is near Har Ksulot and Churchill Forest. An additional scenic road section circles Kibbutz Beit Keshet. It begins at the eastern entrance near Tel Govel, turns toward Mount Deborah (Har Dvora), and after several kilometers the road turns south toward Nahal HaShiv'a and returns to the eastern entrance.
נַחַל שִׁילֹה הוא נחל אכזב בבנימין, אחד:
Nahal Shiloh is an ephemeral stream in the Binyamin region, one of the main tributaries of the Yarkon River. The stream drains 400 square kilometers, which is about 22% of the Yarkon River's drainage basin (1,805 square kilometers).
Nahal Shiloh begins in the east of the Shiloh Valley and flows west, north of El'ad, until it joins the Yarkon River about three kilometers east of the Morasha Interchange. It reaches a length of about 50 kilometers, and alongside it lie impressive heritage, nature and landscape sites, including Nehushonim Forest, Kula Forest, Migdal Afek and Deir Qal'a.
Shmuel Safrai and Amit Shadman hold that in the Second Temple period Nahal Shiloh was a natural border between areas settled by Jews (to the south) and areas settled by Samaritans (to the north).
נַחַל אורן (בערבית: ואדי פלאח) הוא נחל ה:
Nahal Oren (Arabic: Wadi Fallah) is a stream that flows in Mount Carmel. It begins at an elevation of 420 meters above sea level, near the central watershed line of the Carmel in the area of "Horvat Ma'atzera", about two kilometers south-southeast of Isfiya. It is about 14 km long and empties into the Mediterranean Sea north of Atlit. Nahal Oren is the largest of the western drainage basins of the Carmel. Its drainage basin covers about 35 square kilometers. Route 721, which leads from Route 4 to Route 672, runs along the lower western part of the stream's channel.
The stream's drainage basin is composed mainly of rocks from the Cenomanian-Turonian period such as limestone, dolomite and chalk, as well as several tuff outcrops. Most sections of the stream are characterized by a narrow, deep channel.
מַשְׁהַד (בפרסית: ‏‏Ⓘ‏, מילולית: \"מקום:
Mashhad (Persian: Ⓘ, literally "place of martyrdom", related to the Arabic word "shahid") is the second-largest city in Iran and the capital of Razavi Khorasan Province in the northeast of the country. The city is located about 736 km east of the capital Tehran and about 210 km southeast of Ashgabat, the capital of Turkmenistan. Its elevation is 995 meters above sea level.
The city is holy to Shia Muslims because of the Imam Reza Shrine, where the tomb of the eighth Imam, Ali al-Rida, is located (in Persian his name is often pronounced Emam Reza). Millions of Shia believers visit the tomb every year. The city is also known as the city of Ferdowsi, the Iranian poet who wrote the Shahnameh, considered the national epic of Iran, whose tomb is located near the city.
גן לאומי ברעם הוא גן לאומי ובתחומו בית כ:
Bar'am National Park is a national park containing a synagogue from the Talmudic period, whose remains are among the most beautiful built in that era and attest to the existence of a well-established Jewish community at the site. The park extends over a hilltop 755 meters above sea level, overlooking the surrounding area. Kfar Bar'am, the name of the Jewish settlement in which the synagogue stands, is first mentioned in 1210 by the traveler Rabbi Shmuel bar Shimshon, and it apparently came to an end in the Mamluk period.
Within the national park are the buildings of the Arab village of Bir'im, whose residents, Maronite Christians, were evacuated from it during the War of Independence and were not allowed to return afterwards, despite the promises they had received. Over the years the displaced people of Iqrit and Bir'im have waged a legal struggle in the state's institutions demanding to return to their village.
נְתַנְיָה היא עיר במחוז המרכז בישראל, הש:
Netanya is a city in Israel's Central District, the seventh most populous city in the State of Israel. The place was founded by the Bnei Binyamin group in 1929 as a settlement for the sons of the moshavot and for citrus grove workers, and was declared a city in 1948. Netanya is also called the "Capital of the Sharon", because it is the largest city in the Sharon region, and the "Diamond City", because of the developed diamond industry that once existed there.
The city lies on the coastal plain (Central District) on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, on kurkar (calcareous sandstone) ground. The seashore is characterized by high kurkar cliffs along the city's entire coastline, except for its southernmost part – the Poleg neighborhood and Ir Yamim.
The city is named after the philanthropist Nathan Straus, and it is the largest city in Israel whose name commemorates a person.
בקעת קנאים היא בקעה בשולי מדבר יהודה הדר:
Bik'at Kana'im (the Zealots' Valley) is a valley on the southern edge of the Judean Desert, 309 meters above sea level. It is bounded on the east by Har Kana'im, on the west by Har Tzfira, and on the south by Har Menachem. North of it is Nahal Tze'elim, a deep wadi that drops hundreds of meters below the level of the valley; in the section adjacent to the valley lies Birkat Tzfira, which is reached through the valley. It is named after the Zealots who were active during the Great Revolt against the Roman Empire and operated in this area.
In the valley is Kfar HaNokdim, a major holiday village in the area.
Route 3199 crosses the valley in an east–west direction, in its section between Arad and Masada. From it, an unpaved road 3.5 km long branches off along the center of the valley. The Israel National Trail in this section runs between Arad and Masada.
נַחַל בּוֹקֵק (בערבית: وادي البغق או بقق:
Nahal Bokek (Arabic: وادي البغق or بقق or المقلق) is a stream in the Judean Desert about 15 km long, with a catchment area of about 21 square kilometers. The stream descends from Har Ben Nesher and empties onto the shore of the Dead Sea. South of the stream is Nahal Zohar and north of it Nahal Ye'elim. The Dead Sea hotels and the Ein Bokek baths were built on its large alluvial fan. North of the stream's channel, near where it empties into the Dead Sea, stands the Byzantine fortress of Metzad Bokek.
For most of its course the stream runs across the desert plateau, cutting into soft rock (chalk and the Hatrurim Formation), so its valley is shallow. Within the fault escarpment, the stream passes two waterfalls, the first about 100 meters high and the second about 60. After the first waterfall the stream continues flowing through a short (about 1.5 km) deep canyon.
מטע היא יחידת ייצור חקלאית המאופיינת, לר:
A plantation (orchard) is an agricultural production unit characterized, as a rule, by a single agricultural crop. 
Plantations grow various crops such as cotton, tobacco, coffee, sugar cane or fruit trees. Nevertheless, the use of the term "plantation" (mata) is today mainly characteristic of descriptions of tree plantations and orchards.
A plantation is a planned and systematic form of agricultural activity intended to achieve large yields while ensuring optimal use of the land resource and of other inputs such as water, fertilizer, labor, pest control and protection against other threats. Planting is done in rows and columns, which eases the stages of planting, irrigation, care and harvesting. 
In the last generation a method of protection using nets has become common, to reduce damage from birds  and strong wind. In this respect the plantation method is approaching the greenhouse method.
מכתש ירוחם (הגדול; לשעבר המכתש הגדול / מ:
Makhtesh Yeruham (HaGadol; formerly the Large Crater / Makhtesh Hatira) is an erosional crater (makhtesh) located in the eastern Negev in Israel, and one of the five makhteshim of the Negev—similar craters in the region that formed in a similar way, a unique phenomenon that is rare in the world and exists mainly in this area. The makhtesh is elliptical in shape and is the second largest of the Negev makhteshim. It is located in the Hatira anticline, hence its other name.
The makhtesh is 14 km long and 6 km wide. Its maximum depth is 410 meters. The stream that drains it is Nahal Hatira. The makhtesh's boundaries are the Hatira ridge in the west and the Har Karbolet ridge in the east and south, along which the Israel National Trail runs. Northwest of the Large Crater is Har Avnon, rising to a height of 656 meters, from which there is a fine view over the makhtesh.
נְוֵה אָטִי\"ב הוא מושב של תנועת האיחוד:
Neve Ativ is a moshav of the HaIhud HaHakla'i movement on the slopes of Mount Hermon, at an elevation of 950 to 1,050 meters above sea level, about 2 kilometers southwest of Majdal Shams and about 17 kilometers northeast of Kiryat Shmona. It is the third-northernmost settlement in Israel, after Metula and Majdal Shams, and the northernmost settlement in the Golan Regional Council. Route 989 passes through the moshav, where it is called "Sayeret Egoz Boulevard".
The settlement's name is an acronym of the names of four fighters of the Egoz reconnaissance unit who were killed in the course of their military service in the northern Golan Heights: Avraham HaMeiri, Tuvia Sherkinger, Yair Algranti (killed in a military operation near the Oil Road in the Golan on 3 September 1968) and Binyamin Hadad (killed in an ambush near Yardena on 30 April 1968).
עין כרם (בערבית: عين كارم; ההגייה הרשמית: Ein Karem (Arabic: عين كارم; the official pronunciation of the Hebrew name is Ein Kerem, but the common pronunciation is Ein Karem, following the Arabic) is a neighborhood on the southwestern outskirts of Jerusalem. The site was inhabited as early as the Canaanite period; from the 14th century until the War of Independence an Arab village stood there, which was abandoned during the war. New immigrants were settled in the empty houses, and as part of Jerusalem's expansion the village was declared a neighborhood of the city. Even today the neighborhood retains a rural character, owing to its relative separation from the city and its being surrounded by hills, valleys and forests. Ein Karem is also considered a place sacred to Christianity and a pilgrimage site, being known as the birthplace of John the Baptist; there are several churches and monasteries there, visited by many tourists.

The Hatira Ridge or Hatira Anticline is a mountain ridge in the eastern Negev, one of six parallel anticlines in this region whose general orientation is from southwest to northeast, and the highest of them (its peak at 704 meters above sea level). Southeast of the Hatira Ridge is the Oron-Yamin syncline, and northwest of it the Dimona–Yeruham–Sde Boker road (Route 204).
In the Hatira Ridge lies the Large Crater (Makhtesh Gadol), which is an erosional crater. Near the ridge's highest point, at the southwestern end of the makhtesh, there is a monument in memory of Avraham Krinitzi, mayor of Ramat Gan in the 1960s (the road leading from the makhtesh to the monument and the lookout beside it was broken through by the Paratroopers Brigade in 1964, and they named it "Ma'ale Avraham" after Krinitzi, whose city had adopted the paratroopers).

Yardenit is a baptismal site on the Jordan River intended for Christian pilgrims. The site is located south of the river's outlet from the Sea of Galilee, between the Degania Dam and the Alumot Dam near Kvutzat Kinneret, and is owned by the kvutza. The site has 12 separate baptismal pools. In 2012 the site's capacity was doubled in light of the large number of visitors.
According to Christian tradition, John the Baptist baptized Jesus at Qasr al-Yahud, north of the Dead Sea and east of Jericho. For hundreds of years Qasr al-Yahud was an important site for pilgrim visits, and monasteries and hostels were built near it. After the Six-Day War, Qasr al-Yahud became a frontier zone on the border between Israel and Jordan. As a substitute for that site, after the area was declared a closed military zone during the War of Attrition, the Ministry of Tourism initiated the establishment of Yardenit in 1981.
עין ירקעם הוא מעיין עונתי הנובע בחלק העל:
Ein Yorke'am is a seasonal spring that emerges in the upper part of Nahal Hatira, east of the Large Crater (Makhtesh Gadol). The spring flows mainly in winter. In this season the groundwater level rises above ground level (a "tamila"). Usually its waters are also flooded by rainwater and flash floods, filling a large rock pool (gev) to a depth of up to 5 meters. Toward the end of summer little water remains, only in the lower part of the pool, while its upper part dries out, but the spring's groundwater remains relatively high and the animals of the area manage to reach it with a little digging in the sand. The spring is surrounded by abundant vegetation, mainly reeds and tamarisk.
Ancient steps are carved into the wall of the stream's northern bank, which apparently served to bring camels down to drink from the pool. Near the spring is Metzad Yorke'am, a fortress from the Byzantine period that served as a security post.
מאוזוליאום מזור הוא מאוזוליאום רומי מאמצ:
The Mazor Mausoleum is a Roman mausoleum from the mid-3rd century, situated on the western outskirts of the city of El'ad, east of Route 444 and Route 6. The structure stands at an elevation of about 75 meters above sea level, on the northern side of Nahal Mazor. The site on which the structure stands was declared a national park on 21 March 2002 and covers about 25 dunams.
This structure is the only one of its kind in the Land of Israel west of the Jordan to have survived intact from the Roman period. The structure was preserved because for a long period it served as a Muslim place of prayer known as "Maqam an-Nabi Yahya". The structure, 4.8 meters high, is built as a square chamber containing the remains of sarcophagi apparently intended for a married couple. Its ceiling is made of ashlar slabs carried on two arches. Its thick walls and small windows maintain a constant temperature inside.
עמודי עמרם הם עמודים העשויים אבן חול נוב:
Amram's Pillars (Amudei Amram) are pillars made of soft, colorful Nubian sandstone in a pink hue, standing on a cliff at the start of Nahal Amram, at the point where it begins its course toward the Arava. The stream flows in the Eilat Mountains north of Eilat.
The pillars were formed by rainwater cutting into cracks that existed in the cliff. Erosion of the rock along the cracks produced weathering and led to the formation of five tall pillars rising to a height of 15 meters. The hill next to the pillars is called "Givat Yocheved", after Yocheved, the mother of Moses and wife of Amram. The area in which the pillars stand is part of the Eilat Massif Nature Reserve.
The sandstone from which the pillars were formed was created by the weathering of basement rock. The colors that appear in the sandstone are the result of its being washed by water rich in oxides of various materials such as iron, manganese and others.
