Mount Meron (Arabic: جبل الجرمق, Jabal al-Jarmaq) is the highest mountain in the Land of Israel west of the Jordan River and the fourth highest in Israel as a whole. It lies between Safed and Ma'alot-Tarshiha, and its summit rises to 1,204 meters above sea level, the highest point in the Meron range of the Upper Galilee. In the past the mountain rose to 1,208 meters above sea level, but the IDF flattened the summit in order to build an air control unit and lowered it slightly.
Mount Meron is one of the rainiest areas in Israel, receiving on average about 900 millimeters of rain a year. In most winters snow falls on Mount Meron and accumulates. The mountain is covered in Mediterranean maquis that includes oak shrubs, carob, red-trunked strawberry trees (Arbutus andrachne) and others.
Following the Swords of Iron War, before Lag BaOmer the mountain was declared a closed military zone.
תל עזקה (זכריה) הייתה עיר קדומה בליבה של: Tel Azekah (Tell Zakariya) was an ancient city in the heart of the Judean Lowlands (Shephelah). The upper tell is located 347 m above sea level and 117 m above the channel of Nahal HaEla, and its area is about 45 dunams. The tell is located in Britannia Park, managed by KKL-JNF. The site lies at the northern end of a north–south ridge that forms the boundary between the high Shephelah to the east and the low Shephelah to the west. Azekah commands the strategic junction of the road leading from Philistine Gath through the Elah Valley toward the Judean Hills to the east with the road linking Beit Shemesh in the north and Lachish in the south; for these reasons Azekah naturally became an important city. Excavations at the site uncovered remains of settlement mainly from the Late Bronze Age and Iron Age II, a fortress, towers, LMLK seal impressions and other finds. In addition, hiding caves from the period of the Bar Kokhba revolt were discovered at the site.

Mount Shlomo (Har Shlomo), 705 meters high, is one of the oldest mountains in the Eilat Mountains range. Its age is estimated at hundreds of millions of years more than most of the mountains surrounding it. It is about 500 million years older than the adjacent Mount Yehoram.
The mountain is named after King Solomon, who established the mines in the area. Mount Shlomo was meant to be the highest of the mountains named after one of the kings of Judah, but King Hezekiah had a mountain higher than Solomon's named after him, because in Hezekiah's days the Kingdom of Judah's control over this area was restored, after a prolonged revolt by the Edomites.
The mountain is made of magmatic and metamorphic rocks, hence its black color.
The mountain's summit is connected by marked trails to Mount Yehoram, Nahal Shlomo and Route 12, as well as to Nahal Netafim. The marked trails on Mount Shlomo are characterized by especially steep gradients, due to the mountain's overall structure.

Tzova or Palmach Tzova (formerly also called "Tzuba") is a collective kibbutz located in the Jerusalem Corridor, near Mevaseret Zion. The kibbutz sits on a mountain spur 735 meters above sea level, and beside it is Tel Tzova, 769 meters high. The village of Suba, on whose ruins the kibbutz was built, as well as the kibbutz's name, preserve the name of the biblical settlement Zobah, whose remains lie at Tel Tzova.
The kibbutz's economic branches are: industry (the "Oran" factory for automotive safety glass and bullet-resistant glass), and agriculture (including orchards, vineyards, irrigated field crops, olives, tomatoes and hydroponic cabbage grown on water).
In the kibbutz and its surroundings there are many attractions, such as Ein Tzova and its 50-meter-long tunnel, and the Cave of John the Baptist. The kibbutz's tourism branch includes the "Kiftzuba" amusement park for children and the "Tzuba" country hotel. The kibbutz also has a Hebrew-language ulpan.
חוות כנרת (או חצר כנרת) היא חווה חקלאית:
Kinneret Farm (Havat Kinneret, or Kinneret Courtyard) is an agricultural farm established in 1908 on the southwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. It was founded by the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization, at the suggestion of its director, Arthur Ruppin, in order to train Jewish workers in agricultural work and construction for the sake of permanent settlement.
The farm's graduates became the thinkers and founders of the diverse settlement enterprises of the Second Aliyah period and the labor movement: it was here that the first attempts to establish the kvutza, the kibbutz and the moshav began (the settlers of Degania, Kvutzat Kinneret, Nahalal, Ein Harod and others came from it), it became a center of organization for the country's workers, and here the foundations were laid for several organizations that shaped the face of the state-in-the-making, such as the Haganah, HaMashbir, Tnuva and Solel Boneh.
The site was recognized as a heritage site by the Council for Conservation of Heritage Sites in Israel and by the Landmarks (Tzionei Derech) program.
בית גוברין - מָרֵשָׁה הוא גן לאומי שהוכר:
Beit Guvrin-Maresha is a national park declared in 1989 in order to preserve the remains of the city of Maresha, to continue research at the site and to conserve the natural woodland. The national park extends over an area of 5,000 dunams and contains many caves, a variety of underground chambers and important archaeological remains. In the southern and highest part of the park is Tel Maresha.
The bedrock of the Judean Lowlands consists of a layer of chalk, a soft limestone mainly from the Eocene epoch, deposited in an ancient sea. Above the chalk developed a layer 1–3 meters thick of hard limestone known as 'nari'. The chalk bedrock is convenient for quarrying underground chambers and for producing building blocks. Most of the building blocks were quarried from bell-shaped caves with a round opening at the top. Through these openings the quarrymen began their work, quarrying downward row after row and hauling the chalk blocks up for construction purposes.
תֵּל עֲרָד הוא אתר ארכאולוגי בבקעת ערד,:
Tel Arad is an archaeological site in the Arad Valley, about 8 km west of the city of Arad. The tell stands at an elevation of 576 meters above sea level. Tel Arad lies at an important crossroads from the Early Bronze Age to the present day. In the Iron Age, Arad guarded the main road that ran from Jerusalem, Hebron and the Arad Valley toward Horvat Uza and the Dead Sea. Yohanan Aharoni identifies this road with the route of the Way of the Land of Edom (Derekh Eretz Edom).
The tell has two main parts: a large city from the Early Bronze Age, whose remains were visible on the surface even before excavations began; and a fortress on the top of the hill included within this city, dating to Iron Age II (the period of the Monarchy).
Excavations were conducted at the site over 18 seasons, 14 of them in the Early Bronze Age city, headed by Ruth Amiran. A first expedition worked at the site in the years 1962–1966, and the second between 1971 and 1980.

Nahal Peres (Arabic: Wadi Faresh) is an ephemeral stream in the northeastern Negev. It is about 17 km long and flows southeast, parallel to and north of Ma'ale Tamar (Route 25). It begins in Bik'at Tzva'im, about 3 km east of Tzafit Junction, and at its end it empties into Nahal Tamar, about a kilometer and a half east of the Arava Junction.
It is commonly thought that the stream is named after the bird of prey peres (the bearded vulture), but the source of its name is the word "faresh" or "al-faresh" in Arabic, meaning a carpet, mattress or bed, it being a spread-out, enclosed valley suited to camel grazing. The stream is also an ancient Roman road that linked Rafah with the biblical city of Zoar.
In its eastern part the stream flows through a canyon containing rock pools (gevim). In the Ma'ale Peres area, before the confluence with Nahal Tamar, there is a high waterfall of about 50 meters.
Nahal Peres has one tributary – Nahal Tahmas, which originates at Metzad Tamar and meets it at the foot of Har Tzurim.

Jisr az-Zarqa (Arabic: جسر الزرقاء, exact transliteration: Jisr al-Zarqa', sometimes called Jisr for short; in translation: the Blue Bridge) is a local council in the Haifa District of Israel. The village was founded in 1924 and declared a local council in 1961. All the residents of Jisr az-Zarqa are Muslim Arabs.
The town sits on a strip of kurkar (calcareous sandstone) on the Mediterranean coast, 5–20 meters above sea level, at whose foot flows the lower section of Nahal Taninim, which separates the town from the sea to the west. To the south lies Caesarea, and to the north Ma'agan Michael and the entrance to the Nahal Taninim Nature Reserve. To the east the town borders Route 2 (the Haifa–Tel Aviv highway). Near the stream's mouth, southwest of the town's houses, lies Tel Taninim.
The name Jisr az-Zarqa means the Blue Bridge (over the stream), after the bridge built over Nahal Taninim, "al-Wadi az-Zarqa" (the Blue Stream in Arabic).
מפרץ אילת, הידוע מחוץ לישראל כמפרץ עקבה:
The Gulf of Eilat, known outside Israel as the Gulf of Aqaba (Arabic: خليج العقبة), is a long, narrow inlet, a northern arm of the Red Sea separating the Sinai Peninsula from the Arabian Peninsula. The gulf is about 180 kilometers long and its maximum width is 25 kilometers. The gulf's area is 2,880 square kilometers, about 0.5% of the area of the entire Red Sea. The gulf's volume is 2,500 cubic kilometers, about 1% of the volume of the entire Red Sea. Its average depth is 900 meters below sea level and its maximum depth is 1,820 meters below sea level (in the area opposite Nuweiba, near the Saudi coast). Geologically, the Gulf of Eilat is part of the Syrian-African Rift, hence its great depth.
Steep mountains rise on both sides of the Gulf of Eilat – the Sinai mountains to the west and the mountains of Edom and Midian to the east. The average gradient of the gulf floor is 21%, and in certain sections the slope exceeds 50%.
עין לימון, כנראה שיבוש של השם עין לימור,:
Ein Limon, probably a corruption of the name Ein Limor, which is itself a corruption of the name Ein al-Umur (after the village of Khirbet al-Umur that stood nearby), is a layer spring in Nahal Kisalon in the Jerusalem Hills, about a kilometer west of Ein Rafa, at the foot of Har Tzova. On the PEF map and on the 1948 map of the Survey of Israel (the Center for Mapping of the Land of Israel), the spring is called "Ein Mahtush".
Before the War of Independence a village, Khirbet al-Umur, stood at the site, and the pool served its residents. The village sat on a hill about 700 meters west of the spring.
At the site is a small square concrete pool located inside a quarried cutting measuring 18X10 meters, which apparently was the pool in the past. The pool receives its water through a 15-meter-long tunnel that carries the spring water to it. The tunnel and pool are dated to the Roman period in the Land of Israel.
The spring lies on the Israel National Trail, and many hikers tend to stop there to bathe and rest (and some also spend the night at its foot).
נַחַל צִיפּוֹרִי הוא נחל איתן הזורם מהרי:
Nahal Tzipori is a perennial stream flowing from the Nazareth Hills to the Kishon River. The stream, 32 km long, begins its course at the town of Reineh, passes through the hills of Alonim Forest near Shefa-'Amr, and drains into the Kishon River (which in turn drains into Haifa Bay on the Mediterranean coast). It is fed by Einot Tzipori, Einot Yiftah'el and Ein Yivka, and by a large number of intermittent springs such as Ein Rani, Ein Avinoam, Ein Mahil, Ein Gat Hefer, Ein Amat Avel, Ein Lapidot and Ein Tur'an. On old maps such as the Jacotin maps of 1799 and the PEF maps the stream is called Nahar wadi melik, after the wadi in which it flows. Today the name Wadi Milek is attributed to a different wadi. The stream empties into the Kishon near the Bazan (oil refineries) complex.
There is evidence of settlement at the site from thousands of years ago, and along the stream are flour mills and the remains of ancient settlements. Several Bedouin tribes live along the stream in the villages of Zarzir, Ka'abiyye-Tabbash-Hajajre, Khawaled and Hilf.

Mount Deborah (Har Dvora; Arabic: جبل سرطبة, Jabal Sartaba) is a mountain in Israel 437 meters above sea level, located in the Nazareth Hills of the Lower Galilee, on the edge of the Jezreel Valley to its south. It lies between Har Ksulot to the west, Har Yona to the north and Mount Tabor, which is 4.5 km to its southeast. On the mountain's eastern slopes lies the village of Daburiyya, to its west the city of Nof HaGalil, and in the valley to its north the village of Ein Mahil. The mountain's name commemorates the prophetess Deborah, who defeated Sisera, the commander of the army of Jabin king of Hazor, in battle in the valley at its foot.
The mountain is made of limestone and dolomite, and its soil is terra rossa. It is wooded with Mediterranean maquis, especially oak trees. The site was declared a forest reserve as early as the British Mandate period, in 1926, and was called "Sartaba Forest". On the summit KKL-JNF prepared a picnic area, and there stands a rock commemorating the 25th wedding anniversary of Queen Elizabeth II of the United Kingdom and Prince Philip, celebrated in 1972.

The Dead Sea, also known as the Sea of Death (Ⓘ; Arabic: البحر الميت, 'the Dead Sea'), is an endorheic salt lake located within the Syrian-African Rift, with the border between Israel and Jordan running through its center.
The Dead Sea basin consists of two basins, southern and northern. The average depth of the northern basin is about 200 meters, and its floor lies at an average elevation of 730 meters below sea level. The average depth of the southern part was only about ten meters before it dried up, and its floor lay at 401 meters below sea level. Due to the continuing drop in the water level, the southern part of the lake, which was far shallower than the northern one, dried up. Once the southern basin had dried out, evaporation ponds were built in it for the production of potash and other chemicals by the Dead Sea Works in Israel and the Arab Potash Company of Jordan. These ponds require large-scale pumping of the lake's water, and this pumping is among the causes of the drop in the water level.
קֶרֶן נַפְתָּלִי הוא הר בגובה של 510 מטר:
Keren Naftali is a mountain 510 meters above sea level in the Naftali Range of the eastern Upper Galilee, between the Kedesh Valley to the north and the Yahmur Valley to the south. The mountain's eastern slopes drop steeply, within about a kilometer of the summit, to the Hula Valley, which lies at 80 meters above sea level at its foot; from the mountain there is a view over the valley to the Golan Heights and Mount Hermon beyond.
On the summit, remains of a Hellenistic-period fortress, the Keren Naftali fortress, were discovered. Excavations at the site also uncovered remains of a small settlement from the biblical period, and of a larger Hellenistic-Roman temple dedicated to the goddess Athena. Also found at the site were a Greek inscription about a person who donated to the site's upkeep, cisterns, stone walls, burial caves and remains of a mosaic floor. The hilltop may have served as an outpost in the defensive system of Tel Kedesh to its northwest.
The Hasmoneans conquered the site, and the discovery of large stones weighing over 100 kg, which may have been rolled down the slope toward enemy soldiers, hints that a fierce battle was fought here.
Nahal Me'arot is a stream flowing through Mount Carmel. Its drainage basin (together with its tributary Nahal Haruvim) covers about 24 square kilometers. The stream area is a nature reserve within the Carmel Park. At the stream's outlet onto the coastal plain lies an archaeological-prehistoric site of world importance comprising four caves: Tabun (Oven) Cave, Gamal (Camel) Cave, el-Wad (Stream) Cave and Skhul (Kid) Cave. These caves represent repeated occupation by early humans, both Neanderthals and Homo sapiens and their predecessors, over more than half a million years.
The sequence of prehistoric occupation at Nahal Me'arot is exceptionally long and complete. The unique finds discovered at the site (including important human fossils) and its intermittent investigation over more than eighty years have made it one of the world's best-known Paleolithic sites. The four excavated caves yielded evidence, among the earliest in the world, of the coexistence (in the broad sense) of Neanderthals and modern humans; of burial of the dead; of the use of objects with symbolic meaning such as beads and pigments; and of permanent settlement and the building of stone houses.
נַחַל צִין (בערבית: ואדי אל-פִקְרַא) הוא:
Nahal Zin (Arabic: Wadi al-Fiqra) is one of the longest ephemeral streams in Israel (second only to Nahal Paran), and is commonly regarded as the boundary between the northern and central Negev. The stream flows from Mishor HaRuhot north of Makhtesh Ramon, passes south of and below Midreshet Ben-Gurion, and continues from there to the Arava. In the northern Arava the stream is dammed by an earthen embankment, discharges into the drainage systems of the Dead Sea Works and is diverted to the northern basin of the Dead Sea. The stream is about 120 km long, the second-longest ephemeral stream in Israel after Nahal Paran.
Nahal Zin has several names in Arabic, a different one for each section. The first, Wadi Nafah, flows from the Negev Highlands to the point where the wadi turns 90 degrees east (after the Nabataean city of Avdat). The second section is called Wadi Murra, after Ein Mor (the 'bitter spring', named for its brackish water), the lowest spring in the series of springs in the wadi's gorge (after Ein Ma'arif and Ein Avdat). The third section is Wadi Fiqra, which flows from the Ein Avdat canyon to the Dead Sea (the name means 'the poor stream', because of the scarcity of grazing and the few acacia trees in the wadi).

לבן = שלגי החרמון (צפון), כחול = הים/הכנ: White = the snows of Hermon (north), blue = the sea/the Kinneret, orange = the desert (south). According to the popular interpretation, the order of the stripes indicates the walking direction (white toward the north/Hermon, orange toward the south/Eilat).

Near Shizafon/Tzihor and Ovda – active training areas.
הארכת השביל דרך מדבר יהודה: ערד → בקעת ק: Extension of the trail through the Judean Desert: Arad → Kana'im Valley → Masada → Ein Bokek hotels → Metzad Zohar → Nahal Peratzim → Ma'ale Tzurim → Nahal Peres → Nahal Tzafit → the Small Crater (~90 km, 5 segments) instead of Be'er Efe–Metzad Tamar (~40 km). מדרום לערד אין כמעט מקורות מים, ולכן נקב: South of Arad there are almost no water sources, so a system of 'Israel National Trail overnight campsites' was established (sign-only campsites – no water, electricity or toilets), a day's walk apart. Some are accessible to a regular car (convenient for water caching) and some only to 4x4. Paid water-caching services operate from the Arava moshavim (Hatzeva, Tzofar), and at some campsites trail angels cache water (confirm in advance). 5-6 liters per person per day is recommended.

מחשבה רווחת היא שאפשר להשאיר נייר טואלט:
A common belief is that toilet paper can be left in the field because it is biodegradable. True, the paper will indeed decompose; the question is when and under what conditions.
Unlike flushing it down the toilet, where it meets a watery environment, toilet paper we leave behind in nature will remain in the area for one to four months, depending on the amount of precipitation it encounters, the sun's radiation, humidity, etc.
For example, if we are hiking along the Israel National Trail, toilet paper we leave behind at the overnight campsites will still be staining the surroundings long after we have finished hiking the Israel National Trail.
"Getting lost" is the feeling that we have lost our way. If, while walking the trail, we get the feeling that "we have gotten lost", we should check whether we can locate our position on the map and return to the trail route.
If we cannot locate our position in the field, we should retrace our steps to the last point where we were able to orient ourselves, or to the last trail marking we saw. We can also look for the marking in the opposite direction.

– אריזות כבדות כמו קופסאות שימורים המכיל:
– Heavy packaging such as tin cans, which contain a large proportion of liquid – which we will not consume but will have to carry with us as trash until we reach a bin.
– "Wasteful" food that requires gas or water. Foods that need long cooking on a camping stove, such as rice, or boiling water that is poured out after cooking, such as pasta – are in effect a waste of resources that are in short supply when walking a long trail like the Israel National Trail.
– Fresh fruit and vegetables are usually very heavy and contain a high proportion of liquid, and may also get crushed in the pack. Consider reducing their quantities.
– Bread takes up a lot of space in the backpack; it can be replaced with tortillas.
–לא לשטוף כלים במקורות מים. מעיינות ונחל:
–Do not wash dishes in water sources. Springs and flowing streams in Israel serve as drinking water for many wild animals, and in some of them we hikers also like to take a dip now and then. Therefore, it is important to avoid washing dirty dishes in water sources. If necessary, you can take water from the source in a clean container and wash the dirty dish off to the side, not in the water.
– Natural soap is recommended rather than regular dish soap. The dish soap in our kitchen at home goes after use to a sewage treatment plant, where it undergoes a long process until it breaks down and becomes harmless to the environment. But in nature the situation is different: dish soap does not break down and may seep into and pollute the groundwater, as well as the nearby water source.
עדיף אלכוג'ל מים הם משאב מוגבל לעיתים, ב:
Hand sanitizer is preferable. Water is sometimes a limited resource, especially on the southern routes. At some of the campsites there are water tanks with a limited supply of water that is meant to serve many hikers. Therefore, we prefer to disinfect our hands with hand sanitizer and not waste the precious resource.
Soap made from natural ingredients is preferable. If we choose to wash our hands with water, it is important to avoid using soap that is not natural. There are soaps made from natural ingredients that break down well in nature, and are therefore also more suitable for laundry or washing dishes during a hike in nature. By contrast, regular dish soap or hand soap does not break down naturally – and when we use it at home, it goes through a long purification process at the sewage treatment plant near our home.

מטיילים רבים נוטים ללכת בעקבות סימון השב:
Many hikers tend to follow the trail markings "with their eyes closed". But this is a mistake that can lead to getting lost and even to real danger to life.
While hiking, especially on long trails like the Israel National Trail, there are scenarios in which we will find it hard to locate the markings. Problematic weather, such as fog or rain, can make it difficult to find the next marker, as can old markings that still exist in the field. Sometimes the objects on which the trail was marked – such as a fence, a concrete marker post or a rock – may move.
The Israel Trails Committee, led by SPNI, invests great effort every year in maintaining all the existing trail markings in Israel. But it is our responsibility as hikers to use judgment at the moment of truth, to know the route in advance, and not to rely solely on the markings in the field.
ימי הטיול בשביל ישראל ובשבילים אחרים הם:
Hiking days on the Israel National Trail and other trails are often long and hot. It is therefore worth preparing in advance and knowing the points along the day's walk where water can be refilled.
Points for refilling and stocking up on water are usually found in the communities near the trail, at gas stations and at cemeteries, which can be relied on with high certainty (except on unusual days such as holidays and festivals, when shops are sometimes closed).
However, taps and water tanks scattered along the Israel National Trail and other trails – for example at overnight campsites, in parks and in nature reserves – may be out of order or empty. Therefore, before setting out on the route, it is recommended to check on the various platforms (seasonal WhatsApp groups of Israel National Trail hikers, Facebook groups, online forums and more) whether the water points we intend to rely on are in working order.
ערב ההליכה ובבוקר יום הטיול יש לוודא שתח:
On the evening before the hike and on the morning of the hike itself, make sure the updated weather forecast allows walking the route and does not put us at risk. For example, there are segments along the Israel National Trail that are not recommended for walking when rain is likely or after rain, and may even be dangerous.
For this purpose, it is worth getting to know the Israel Meteorological Service website, where you can check warnings for the specific day of the hike.
When you enter the site, the evening before the hike and again on the morning of the hike itself, look for the word "Warnings" that appears on the home screen, at the top left.
After clicking the "Warnings" button, a page with a map of Israel will open.
An area shown on the map in green indicates that there are no warnings for that place at the time we searched.
If there are yellow, orange or red areas on the map, it means there is a warning for the hiking area. It is important to open the warning and understand what is causing it, and accordingly consider whether it is appropriate to go hiking in the area at that time.
בסיום המדורה, יש לוודא שהיא כבויה לחלוטי:
When finishing the campfire, make sure it is completely extinguished – whether by pouring water on it or by urinating on it. On hot, dry days it is important to check several times that the fire has been completely put out, while moving the coals and turning them over.
If we did not light the campfire in a pit, as is recommended, dig a pit and move the remains of the embers and ash into it. Then cover the pit with soil, gaining two benefits: making sure the fire is out, and clearing the area of the campfire's "scars".
Mark the pit with a stick or stones. After we have buried the embers and covered the pit, mark the pit with a stick, a board or stones. The marking is needed because in the first hours the embers remain hot. Even though we covered them with soil, the soil also heats up, and this way we prevent others from sitting down on the spot and getting burned.
If we used wooden pallets, it is important that we also collect the nails after us. Nails are a nuisance and the overnight campsites are full of them. The metal will not decompose, so we collect this tiny waste after us too.
האתגרים הפיזיים והמנטליים בטיול ארוך הם:
The physical and mental challenges of a long hike are big enough as it is, so why hike alone at all?
The choice to hike solo can stem from several reasons. First of all, even if we really try, we won't always manage to arrange in advance whom to hike with. Many hikers set out alone on long trails – after struggling to find someone to take the first step with, but not wanting to give up on the adventure.
Another reason to hike a long trail alone is the desire to experience walking in solitude – the empowering and complex experience of overcoming the physical and mental challenge it involves. There are also those who want to withdraw from the world, spend time with themselves and clear their heads.
Whatever the reason, experiencing a long hike alone can be a wonderful experience, and our chances of enjoying it will rise the better we prepare ourselves for the challenges and difficulties that may arise. That is exactly why we prepared this guide to solo hiking.

מרבית המגבונים מיוצרים מאל-בד, שהוא למעש:
Most wipes are made of non-woven fabric, which is in fact a fabric made from a synthetic material called polypropylene – and it takes a long time to disappear from the field. How long is a long time? A wipe left in nature will take an average of 500 years to disappear!
Even wipes marketed as biodegradable and made from plant-based materials break down imperfectly and very slowly. So no matter how it is marketed to us, the wipes we leave behind will not vanish as if they never existed. It is therefore recommended to avoid using them. If we really insist on using wipes, we collect them in a trash bag and throw them in the nearest bin instead of leaving them in nature.
Like wipes, disposable sanitary pads and tampons are also made of materials that do not decompose easily. Here too it is a matter of an enormous span of hundreds of years until they decompose. Therefore, when we use these products, it is important to pack them in a trash bag and throw them in the nearest bin.

מזמן מזמן, לפני כ-1.5 מיליון שנה, האדם ה:
Long, long ago, about 1.5 million years ago, humans began to learn to light fire and control it. Since then, fire has played an important role in the development of human society, helping to provide light, heat, roasting and cooking, and expanding the range of food people consume – a fact that probably contributed to the development of our brain.
Today we use electrical appliances at home, but in the moments when we get away from home, the need to light a campfire arises: to keep warm, to prepare food, or even just for the atmosphere and social bonding.
Sitting by a campfire after a long day of walking is a moment of contentment, warmth and respite on a long journey. That said, it is important to remember that if we do not act carefully, the campfire could, heaven forbid, cause a wildfire and serious environmental damage. Since in any case we will also be carrying a camping stove, cookware and a flashlight, and we probably won't need a campfire for cooking and light, it is recommended to consider whether this is the right place and time to light a fire, and to refrain from doing so if the conditions are not suitable.
If we have decided to light a campfire, here is a guide that explains exactly how to do it – so that we can enjoy it without causing any damage to the environment.
הכל תלוי בנו, ובבחירה איפה ומתי נטייל. י:
It all depends on us, and on the choice of where and when we hike. Israel is a small, crowded country. To disappear into the wilderness and meet no people at all, you have to try very hard.
On most routes we will meet other hikers, mainly in the hiking seasons of autumn and spring. Abroad too there are long trails that are popular and heavily touristed, but also ones where you can choose to be alone in peace.
Assuming that all of us would be glad of some company now and then, whether while walking or at the overnight campsite, we can add playing cards, for example, to the gear list, and learn a few games in advance that will pass the time and ease the awkwardness of meeting new people.
In general, it is worth overcoming the awkwardness, approaching and striking up a conversation with the hikers we meet. Some of us find this difficult and for some it feels natural; either way, developing the ability to connect with new people and build relationships from scratch is an important experience in itself, and even an opportunity to acquire life skills.
Many hikers who started walking alone formed new and interesting connections along the trail, and there are even friendships that were formed on the journey and continued long after it ended.
להתרחק ממקורות מים בחיפושנו אחר מקום שקט:
Keep away from water sources. In our search for a quiet, secluded spot to relieve ourselves, it is recommended to keep away from people and also from water sources. It is very important to keep water sources clean: for the sake of hikers who purify water on the routes in various ways (abroad, hikers even allow themselves to simply drink from the streams), and of course for the sake of the wild animals that come to drink from the streams and springs – around which there is a whole environment of animals and plants that depend on them. So let us adopt the habit of moving at least 90 steps away from a water source when we want to relieve ourselves in nature.
Bury your waste. Found a secluded, quiet spot far from a water source? Now dig a small hole using a small trowel we brought with us from home in advance, or a stick we found in the field. The hole should be at least 10 cm deep.
After digging a suitable hole, do your business inside the hole, and if we missed, move it into the hole with a stick and cover it with soil. Finally, place a large rock on the hole to keep the soil from being exposed and to keep others from digging in the same spot.
Collect toilet paper in a bag. The toilet paper we used is collected in a trash bag, tied up and thrown in the nearest bin.
לפני היציאה לטיול, כדאי לפתוח מפת סימון:
Before setting out on a hike, it is worth opening a trail-marking map and studying the route.
Start and end point. We locate the start and end points and measure the distance between them. Measuring the distance will give us a first hint of what our day will look like: can we take our time, or will we need to hurry, or perhaps even shorten the route.
For example, an average person walking on flat terrain without special gear walks at a pace of 3 km per hour. However, each of us has a personal walking pace that is affected by fitness level, pack weight, the number of breaks we take along the way, etc.
Terrain. Another factor that affects walking pace is topography. Look at the contour lines on the trail-marking map: are they close together? Dense contour lines indicate steep terrain. Steep climbs, as well as sharp descents, may take more time than a leisurely walk on flat ground.
What else can we learn from the map? The map shows other symbols from which we can learn about our route: will we be walking through wooded, shaded terrain, or is the walk exposed to the sun? Does the route pass along the edge of a firing zone, a minefield or a nature reserve? Is there a main road on the way, and if so, how does the trail get around it? And also: what are the possible evacuation routes in case of an emergency, where are the nearby communities suitable for stocking up, springs for a refreshing dip, points of interest along the route and more.
אתגר פיזי. בכל טיול ארוך יש ציוד שלא נוכ:
Physical challenge. On every long hike there is gear we cannot do without, whether we hike alone or in a group. Cookware, a camping stove, spices, a first-aid kit, and sometimes a tent too – these are items a pair or a group can share, both in use and in their backpacks, whereas on a solo hike there is no one to share with and we have to load everything onto ourselves, in both senses.
Mental challenge. Even on a group hike or a hike as a pair there are quite a few mental challenges, related to our place within the group, communication with others in better and worse moments, disagreements and decision-making. These challenges can become the advantages of hiking alone – but they are joined by difficulties that those who hike in a group do not encounter.
If we set out on a hike alone, we will not have to deal with the wishes of others, but we also won't benefit from advice in moments of crisis. We won't have to work on our communication with others in the middle of a hard walk, but we will have to improve our communication with ourselves and our awareness of the difficult physical and emotional sensations that will come along the way, such as fear, uncertainty, frustration, boredom, anger and disappointment. Along with them will come positive and pleasant feelings too, but there will be no one to share those with either.
Dealing with an emergency. One of the biggest fears about setting out on a long hike alone is the chance of ending up in an emergency. Situations of no cell reception, distance from roads and communities, or, heaven forbid, a medical emergency – can pose a serious challenge even for hikers in a group, and certainly for someone hiking alone.
– מזון יבש וקל המכיל כמות קלוריות וחלבון:
– Dry, light food with a large amount of calories and protein. We prefer food that can be cooked with relatively little water and in a short time. For example, couscous, red lentils, oats, ptitim (Israeli couscous), instant mashed potato powder or quick-cook noodles.
– Dried fruit and nuts provide energy and contain less liquid, so they are lighter than fresh fruit.
– Tuna in a pouch is a good source of protein, and to reduce packaging weight and trash volume we prefer it packed in a pouch.
– Instant soup powders for warming up on cold evenings or as an addition to a meal; can be upgraded with noodles.
– Milk powder is a good source of protein on long walking days.
– Brewer's yeast adds flavor and a creamy effect to dishes, resembling Parmesan in texture and taste.
– Tortillas take up less space than bread, for example.
– Nori seaweed for sushi is lightweight and upgrades any carbohydrate dish.
– Cheeses with a high fat percentage tend to hold up in the backpack through the day, in the winter season and on cold days.
– Spreads: prefer to take them in packaging that is as lightweight as possible, and avoid heavy glass jars.
– Sauces: take them in small quantities and transfer them to small bottles or test tubes, if available. A few examples: soy sauce, chili sauce, agave syrup.
– Seasoning cubes: ready-made tablets with concentrated spices in various flavors.

Here are our trail recipes for long-distance hikes!
The quantities in the recipes are for an average portion; you can add/reduce to taste and according to how hungry you are.
Nutritious and tasty oatmeal porridge
Ingredients for one portion:
– 4 tablespoons fine rolled oats
– 0.75 cup water
– 1 tablespoon milk powder
– 1 teaspoon sugar
– some dried fruit/nuts for an upgrade
Preparation:
1. Boil 0.75 cup of water.
2. Meanwhile, mix all the dry ingredients in a bowl.
3. Once the water has boiled, add the hot water to the bowl – and stir well.
Buddha bowl
Ingredients for one portion:
– a third/half cup of rice (depending on hunger)
– nori seaweed for sushi
– soy sauce
– salt to taste
– you can add a piece of vegetable such as cabbage, pepper, carrot, etc.
Preparation:
1. Boil water in a quantity twice that of the rice.
2. Once the water is boiling, add the rice and seasonings, stir and cover.
3. Continue cooking over low heat for 15 minutes.
4. At the end of the cooking time, turn off the heat and let the pot rest for a few minutes.
5. Chop the vegetable (if you have one) and mix it with the rice in the bowl/pot.
6. Tear the sushi seaweed by hand, mix with the rice and add soy sauce.
Indulgent risotto
Ingredients for one portion:
– a handful of dried mushrooms
– half/a third cup of rice (depending on hunger)
– a piece of high-fat cheese, such as processed cheese of any kind or hard cheese
– salt to taste
– olive oil
– a small disposable plastic bottle
– a knife
Preparation:
1. 6 hours before the meal, put the dried mushrooms into a small plastic bottle and fill it with water to the top. Close the bottle tightly with the cap and "forget" about it until mealtime.
2. Fill the pot with the mushroom water and the mushrooms (you can cut the bottle open for this), and bring the water to a boil with the mushrooms inside.
3. Once the water has boiled, add olive oil, and then the rice.
4. Make sure the rice is covered with water at all times, and continue cooking and stirring until the rice is done.
5. When the rice is cooked and hot, add the processed cheese and stir.
Trail bulgur salad
Ingredients for one portion:
– half a cup of bulgur
– half a cucumber
– a tomato
– a little olive oil
– lemon juice (if available)
– salt and pepper to taste
– a small disposable plastic bottle
– a knife
Preparation:
1. 3 hours before the meal, fill the bottle
נבין מהם הצרכים שלנו האם אני מתכננת טיול:
Understand your needs Am I planning a long hike on the Israel National Trail? Am I looking for a pack for day hikes? Based on that, we will try to understand what need the pack is meant to meet, and thus work out the desired volume and which features are more or less important. Below you will find explanations and information about the various properties and features, and about the right way to plan the packing of your gear inside the pack.
It is important to understand that a week-and-a-half trip will require a pack volume similar to one suited to a two-month trip. This is because in any case we will stock up on food and water as we walk, and we will wash our clothes during the trip.
Make a list of the items that should go into the pack Once we have understood our needs, we will work out what needs to be packed. The idea is to understand how much space all these items will take up. Remember that some gear takes up more volume, such as a sleeping bag, mattress, cooking kit, etc.
Based on the expected quantity and size of the gear that will go into the pack, we can choose the appropriate volume. Preparing a list in advance will prevent disappointment. If we buy a pack that is too small, we will have to hang many items on the outside of the pack, which will get in the way of walking. On the other hand, if we buy a pack that is too big – we will probably be tempted to fill it with non-essential gear that adds unnecessary weight to our back. Below we explain how it is recommended to plan the gear you need.
Straps Hiking packs are usually loaded with straps from every compartment and in every direction, and it is very easy to get lost. But there are several straps worth knowing:
– The hip belt is designed to ensure that the pack's weight is split between the shoulders and the hips, so make sure it closes without pressing on the stomach and "sits" on us well.
– The pack's shoulder straps put the weight on the shoulders, and the straps above them are meant to pull the upper part of the pack toward the shoulder blades when needed.
– Beyond these, when trying on the pack make sure all the other straps on the pack are closed and tightened, which "packs" the pack and compresses it.
Features After we have tried on the pack with weight and volume and made sure the main straps are comfortable and suit us, we move on to features. Here there is no limit to creativity: a compartment for a hydration bladder, a compartment for water bottles on the side or front, small pockets for snacks, compartments for sandals, a zipper along the sides of the pack so it opens like a suitcase, straps for tying on a mattress, and what not.

נבדוק מה מסתתר מתחת לאף אחותך חזרה מהטיו:
Check what is hiding right under your nose Has your sister come back from her big trip and no longer uses her backpack? Is there a pack your uncle does not need hiding in his storeroom? Our acquaintances may well have an unused hiking pack at home that could suit us.
Join second-hand groups Like many other hobbies, hiking may also require buying expensive gear. Buying second-hand will be cheaper – and more ecological too. The second-hand market for hiking gear in Israel offers a range of products, even if it is not as developed as abroad, and the groups on the subject are active mainly on Facebook.
Try packs on properly in the store If we have chosen to buy in a store, the chance of choosing the most suitable pack grows the more packs we try on, and the better we understand what is more or less comfortable for us. There are many brands on the market offering packs with a variety of back systems suited to different body types. For example, people with a narrow, short build will suit a different back system than people with a broad, tall build.
When trying on a pack in the store, ask to add weight to the pack. Most outdoor stores keep sandbags of various weights, and if there are none, you can fill the pack with relatively heavy, bulky products. Trying on the pack with weight inside is meant to simulate real use of the pack on the trail, which will usually include at least 3 liters of water, clothing for the season, food, a sleeping bag, cooking utensils and more. After adding weight to the pack, we may discover that a pack that seemed comfortable is not, and sometimes it turns out that the added weight makes the pack more comfortable.
The bigger the pack, the more it will weigh On long trails, the key word is minimalism – that is, carry as little as possible and try to choose the lightest gear you can. The larger the volume of the pack we choose, the greater the chance that we will fill it with non-essential things and weigh ourselves down.
More expensive is not better A hiking pack does not have to be an expensive affair, and there is a chance that an expensive pack will not suit our needs at all. Of course some brands are of higher quality than others, but in the end comfort is the deciding factor. If the pack is comfortable and sits well on us, we may have found the right pack, even if it is not made by a prestige brand.

מילת המפתח: מינימליזם ככל שנעמיס פחות הת:
The key word: minimalism The less we load, the less the pack weighs – and the more fun we will have hiking. Before packing, it is worth laying out in front of us all the items we want to take, going through them one by one and checking: is it essential? If there is an item that can be weeded out – one less shirt, one less pair of socks, etc. – don't hesitate to give it up. Remember that every unnecessary gram adds to the already heavy weight on our back and affects the quality of the trip and our enjoyment.
Plan ahead as much as possible What will we eat at each meal and what ingredients are needed? For example, instead of putting a 1 kg bag of rice in the pack, check in advance how many meals you will need, how many portions you will cook and where the next resupply point is – and accordingly pack only the necessary amount according to the plan.
The same goes for water: in the north there are many points where you can stock up on water during the day, so you can carry less water – as long as you plan ahead.
Sleeping bag The sleeping bag is without doubt one of the most important items we pack for the trip. Compress the sleeping bag as small as possible using its straps. If the sleeping bag came in a cover without straps, it is recommended to buy a compression sack, which will save us a lot of space. Most hiking packs have a bottom compartment where a compressed sleeping bag can usually be packed comfortably. In winter or on days when rain is expected, it is recommended to put the sleeping bag in a plastic bag, to make sure that when we reach the campsite in the evening we have a dry sleeping bag to get into.
Heavy items Heavy items, such as a pot, heavy food packages, etc., should be packed in the compartment above the sleeping bag compartment – as close as possible to our back and at the bottom of the compartment. This is the area where the hip belt provides good support, so it is best to place the heavy gear there. Avoid putting heavy items in the part of the pack close to the head or far from the back, to keep your balance and not overload the shoulders.
Mattress Although a camping mattress is usually lightweight compared to other items we carry on our back on the trip, it takes up a lot of volume, so it is worth thinking in advance about its place in the pack. There are two main types of camping mattress. The "egg-crate" mattress that folds like an accordion, or closed-cell foam mattresses – are usually tied on the outside, at the bottom or on the sides of the pack, using the straps. האתגרים בטיול לבד הם רבים – אבל אם הרעיו:
The challenges of hiking alone are many – but if the idea appeals to you, it is not worth giving up the experience. There are ways to cope with the difficulties and increase the chance that a solo hike will be not only about overcoming challenges, but also a very special kind of enjoyment.
Here are 7 tips that can help:
1. Start by thinking things over with ourselves. Try to work out the reasons that make us want to hike alone, and then answer honestly questions such as how well we know ourselves in moments of crisis and what usually helps us get through them, how comfortable we will feel in nature both in daylight and when darkness falls, whether we have hiking experience, and if so what kinds of hikes we have tried in the past, and which skills we would like to improve before setting out on such an adventure.
2. Learn basic fieldcraft skills. You don't need to be a scout instructor to hike by yourself for a week in nature, but it is worth knowing how to read a topographic map with a scale, navigate without an app, use a camping stove, pitch a tent and light a fire, for example.
3. Try a short solo hike to begin with. To get a first idea of what it feels like to hike alone, choose an easy route that includes one or two nights and requires us to carry gear on our back and sleep outdoors. Since this is a first experience, soften it with a relatively well-traveled route, where we may walk alone but will not really be alone, and will at least have the option of sleeping in the company of others.
It should be a route with cell reception and exit points along the way, in case we find the experience unpleasant, and preferably one where we can stock up on food along the way and not just water, to lift our spirits and ease the load on our back.
4. Arrange for someone at home to receive updates from us. It is important that someone at home knows in advance where and when we will be hiking, and that we update them several times a day or as much as possible. That way, in an emergency without reception, at the very least there will be someone who will make sure to look for us.
5. Learn about the area we will hike in. Unfamiliarity heightens feelings of fear and anxiety (and this is true in every area of life). Of course confidence comes with experience, but learning about the area and surroundings in advance can help. That way, if we wake up at night to unusual sounds, we will know in advance that it is most likely just a cow or a wild boar, that the howls of the jackals at dusk do not mean they are coming to devour us, and what
1. נביא איתנו את חומרי הבעירה. חשוב שנבי:
1. Bring your own fuel. It is important to bring fuel with us so as not to damage the local vegetation – damage that occurs even if we gather "just" a few branches from a tree or bush. In addition, it is important to avoid burning synthetic materials, or wood with a coating or chemical treatment, such as spraying against woodworm or paint.
2. Make sure lighting a fire is permitted. Before lighting a campfire, it is important to make sure that lighting fires is permitted where we are. For example, lighting fires is prohibited in nature reserves, unless signage on site explicitly states that it is permitted. Sometimes, in transitional seasons and due to unusual weather, the Fire Commissioner issues a "campfire ban order", which is published online. If we suspect that this may be such a time, it is important to check and make sure. In the era of climate change, the weather in Israel is becoming hotter and drier and there are more fire-prone days throughout the year. Extra caution is therefore required on this matter.
3. Check whether there is a designated campfire area. Some overnight campsites have designated campfire and fire-lighting areas, in order to concentrate the campfires in defined spots and keep the overnight campsite cleaner. If there is a designated fire-lighting area, it should be preferred.
4. Check whether there are remains of existing campfires. If there are no designated campfire areas, it is better to light the fire on the remains of a previous campfire. There are two reasons for this: first, in many cases coals that did not burn completely can be used as fuel; and second, campfires often leave "scars" on the ground, such as the marks of the fire including the coals, the ash and also the low grasses next to the fire that the flames consume as it burns. It is unpleasant to sleep on this mess and unfortunately the overnight campsites are full of it, so it is better to use the remains of an existing campfire and not create additional "scars" in the area.
5. If there are no remains of existing campfires, dig a pit for the campfire. It is better to light the campfire in a pit, which will help contain it and later also cover it and remove the mess.
6. Make sure the campfire is not under a tree or next to bushes. To prevent sparks from reaching tree branches and low leaves, keep it away from them.
7. There is no need to ring the campfire with stones. Although this is a popular solution, ringing the campfire with stones is not useful and may even create a hazard. Certain rocks

How do we light the fire? Matches or a lighter are the most convenient option. A fire can also be lit using a fire steel, but it is heavier and requires a high level of skill.
Gathering tinder: To light the campfire we will need flammable materials found around us. Dead, dry grasses, pine needles and even the toilet paper we used during the day. If nothing is available, you can use a good knife to cut thin wood shavings from the fuel we brought in advance, such as pieces of wood and pallets we planned to burn in the campfire.
Fuel: To protect the natural vegetation around the overnight campsite, we avoid at all costs breaking branches and damaging trees or bushes. Think for a moment what would happen if each and every one of us broke just one branch, and remember that even a rotting tree trunk decomposing on the ground has environmental meaning and importance – for example, it serves as a home and food for a variety of insects and fungi, which are part of the area's biodiversity.
The fuel needs to be dry, and it can be obtained by collecting leftovers from other campfires at the campsite and wooden pallets that jeep drivers sometimes leave behind, or through "caches". At the campsites in the south, in addition to water bottles, you can also buy sacks of firewood for campfires from the water-caching providers.
Lighting the campfire: Kneel next to the spot where we want to light the fire, and prepare piles of tinder and fuel to one side, in order. First, prepare a pile of the thinnest and most flammable tinder (such as wood shavings, pine needles or toilet paper). Then add small dry twigs we found on the ground, and finally the fuel that is meant to burn for a long time, such as planks.
There are various methods of fire engineering, and the simplest of all is probably the tepee or pyramid method. Pile up, from the inside out: easily ignited material at the bottom, and above it twigs from small to large. Make sure the whole time that the pyramid is ventilated enough for the oxygen essential for burning to get in.
Once the pyramid is ready, light the most flammable materials at the bottom. Usually, when done right, the fire catches and spreads from the most flammable materials to the twigs. In practice, sometimes you need to add more of the most flammable material until the fire catches on the twigs, or blow gently at the fire from below.
